articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Fable 5.1: Fewer refusals, with small savings on the login fix
articles.text:
Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Fable 5.1: Fewer refusals, with small savings on the login fix
Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 promises fewer refusals and lower token prices, but those changes played out very differently in our head-to-head coding comparisons.
Anthropic compared Fable 5.2 with its predecessor, Fable 5.1, on safeguard blocks, output speed, and API pricing. The company states that Fable 5.2 triggered about 55% fewer safeguard blocks than Fable 5.1 overall and about 60% fewer in cybersecurity in early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork. It also says Fable 5.2 generates output up to 30% faster and lists standard API rates of $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Both rates are 20% lower than Fable 5.1’s $10 and $50.
I compared Fable 5.2 and Fable 5.1 on three developer tasks and tracked refusals, accuracy, tokens, estimated cost, and elapsed time. The comparison uses one run per model for each task or version, including the October Fable 5.1 webhook result. That’s a small sample, and the API runs used a different setup from Anthropic’s safeguard testing.
The tests
For the new runs, I used Anthropic’s API with the default effort setting of High for both models, with no turn cap or fallback model. A script graded every run against an answer key I created for the tests. The dollar figures are estimated API costs. Anthropic prices uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, and output separately.
- Webhook chat: I reused a 50-turn scripted chat that I first ran on Fable 5.1 in October. It simulates a dev lead building a small webhook relay. The chat contains 25 project rules, eight of which change later and three of which are only implied. At the end, the model writes the config and code and then takes an eight-question recall quiz.
- Signature checker: I gave each model a written spec for code that verifies signed webhooks, rejects replays, and rate-limits senders, and then sent a change request. A hidden suite of 50 tests graded the final code output.
- Login repo fix: Each model worked as an agent in a small login library with interacting bugs in passwords, lockouts, reset tokens, and sessions. The library also had one wrong test that the model should report but not edit.
Webhook chat
In the October Fable 5.1 run I’m using for comparison, the API refused 34 of 50 turns. The first refusal came on turn 5, when I asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable. In that October run, I kept my prompts in the chat history and discarded refused model responses. Fable 5.1 also refused the final code and the quiz, so it scored zero on both. The task was to build an ordinary backend relay.
The first refusal came on turn 5, when I asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable.
Fable 5.2 finished the same script without a refusal. That gave me a complete run to grade for long-conversation recall. Its code used the most recent version of all eight rules, which changed midway, and on the quiz it answered “unknown” to the three questions that had no answer. Fable 5.2 didn’t fill gaps with guesses.
The numbers:
• Fable 5.2: 50 turns, 298,709 in, 41,828 out (28,550 reasoning), $4.06, 427 s.
• Fable 5.1 (October): 34 of 50 turns refused, with no code or quiz answers.
Signature checker
Fable 5.1 refused both turns of this test in under a second each, and the API labeled both refusals “cyber.” The spec asked for code that verifies signed webhooks, rejects replays, and rate-limits senders. The API returned no output on either turn. Anthropic says benign security work can trigger its cyber classifier.
Fable 5.2 took the same spec, handled the change request, and passed all 50 hidden tests, including the edge cases on timestamps, rotated secrets, and replays.
The numbers:
- Fable 5.2: 2 turns, 21,299 in, 26,167 out (18,407 reasoning), $1.22, 253 s.
- Fable 5.1: 2 turns, both refused, 3,206 reported input tokens, 0 output tokens, $0.00 under Anthropic’s billing rules for cyber refusals before output, 2 s.
Login repo fix
This was the one test where both models completed the work, showing how they compare once refusals are out of the picture. The models kept getting perfect scores, so I made the tests harder and reran them twice. Here’s what differed between the tests:
- Version 1: The library had bugs in four modules that handle password hashing, lockouts, reset tokens, and sessions. It also had one wrong test.
- Version 2: I added a one-time-code module with its own bugs and tightened the rules in the existing modules. Usernames had to match across Unicode forms, and sessions had to handle a clock that runs backward.
- Version 3: I added an audit log that must redact secrets and a rate limiter. Neither module came with any tests.
The models tied on all three versions of the login repo fix. Both scored 50/50 on each version, fixing the bugs the grader covered and reporting the wrong test without editing it.
Fable 5.1 never refused on the login repo fix, even though the task covered passwords, lockouts, and reset tokens.
Across the three versions, dividing total output tokens (including reasoning) by total elapsed time gives about 107 tokens per second for Fable 5.2 and 82 for Fable 5.1. The elapsed time includes the entire task run. Fable 5.2 took four turns on each version, while Fable 5.1 took 7, 21, and 25. Fable 5.2 also produced more reasoning tokens on each version.
Fable 5.2 finished the first two versions faster and at a lower estimated cost. It took longer and cost more on the third.
The numbers:
- Version 1
  - Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 16,149 in, 4,502 out (1,178 reasoning), $0.27, 43 s.
  - Fable 5.1: 7 turns, 33,935 in, 4,761 out (1,149 reasoning), $0.36, 52 s.
- Version 2
  - Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 24,081 in, 10,024 out (4,887 reasoning), $0.56, 95 s.
  - Fable 5.1: 21 turns, 139,189 in, 9,475 out (4,018 reasoning), $0.68, 118 s.
- Version 3
  - Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 34,269 in, 17,964 out (10,578 reasoning), $0.96, 166 s.
  - Fable 5.1: 25 turns, 208,826 in, 10,638 out (4,342 reasoning), $0.79, 132 s.
Results
The token, cost, and time totals below cover the signature checker and all three login repo versions. Fable 5.1 produced no output on the signature checker, while Fable 5.2 spent 253 seconds and an estimated $1.22 completing it. Across the three login versions that both models completed, elapsed time and estimated cost were close. The combined totals include the work only Fable 5.2 completed on the signature checker.
| Test | Claude Fable 5.2 | Claude Fable 5.1 | 
| Webhook chat refusals (of 50) | 0 | 34 (October) | 
| Webhook chat code and quiz | 25 of 25, 8 of 8 | 0 of 25, 0 of 8 (October) | 
| Signature checker (of 50) | 50 | 0, both turns refused | 
| Login repo fix, 3 versions (of 150) | 150 | 150 | 
| Tokens in / out, signature checker and login fix | 95,798 / 58,657 | 385,156 / 24,874 | 
| Estimated cost, signature checker and login fix (sum of displayed estimates) | $3.01 | $1.83 | 
| Total time, signature checker and login fix (sum of displayed times) | 557 s | 304 s | 
What do I think?
In my tests, the biggest improvement with Fable 5.2 was fewer refusals. Fable 5.1 blocked ordinary webhook and signature-checking work, and Fable 5.2 completed both without a single refusal. Anthropic says the newer model still uses cyber safeguards.
In my tests, the biggest improvement with Fable 5.2 was fewer refusals.
Across the three login repo versions, Fable 5.2 produced about 30% more output tokens per second of elapsed time, including reasoning, while taking about the same total time. The runs took 304 seconds in total on Fable 5.2 and 302 seconds on Fable 5.1.
The displayed cost estimates add up to $1.79 and $1.83, respectively, a savings of about 2% for these runs. Anthropic’s 20% price cut applies to its standard per-token rates. I ran each version once per model, so I’d try both on your own workload to see what the numbers look like for you.
Learning Path

articles.title: Casi el 30% de la generación Z usa IA sin conocimiento de sus jefes
articles.text:
Casi un tercio de los trabajadores de la generación Z, el 29%, utiliza inteligencia artificial en su empleo sin que sus superiores lo sepan, una práctica que la división Imperial Lifelong Learning del Imperial College London denominó “IA en la sombra”. La cifra supera en 11 puntos a la de los millennials, que se ubica en el 18%, y más que duplica la registrada entre la generación X.
El hallazgo forma parte de un informe que encuestó a 2.000 trabajadores de cinco sectores: servicios financieros; ingeniería, manufactura e infraestructura; tecnología y digital; energía y sostenibilidad; y salud y ciencias de la vida. El estudio describe la relación de la generación Z con estas herramientas como “compleja”: aunque el 48% las usa de forma habitual en su trabajo, más de un tercio asegura sentir que recurrir a la IA resulta deshonesto.
El uso regular varía según la generación
Los datos muestran diferencias notables en la frecuencia de uso entre generaciones. Los millennials encabezan la lista, con un 55% que emplea IA de manera habitual en sus tareas laborales. Les sigue la generación Z con el 48%, un porcentaje más cercano al de la generación X (45%) que al de los propios millennials. Los baby boomers presentan el uso más bajo, con un 31%.
Pese a que la generación Z no es el grupo que más utiliza estas herramientas, sí es el que expresa mayor inquietud sobre las percepciones ajenas. El 26% de estos trabajadores cree que sus colegas o superiores los verán de forma negativa por usar IA, una preocupación que, según el informe, también comparten los millennials pese a ser el grupo con mayor adopción.
Un informe que detecta brecha de habilidades
El estudio identificó una preocupación transversal a todas las generaciones: el 59% de los encuestados considera que existe una brecha de habilidades en la industria donde trabaja.
Dos tercios, el 66%, cree que la competitividad internacional del Reino Unido se verá afectada si este problema no se aborda, y el 70% sostiene que, de no cerrarse la brecha, se reducirán las oportunidades laborales disponibles para la próxima generación dentro de los próximos cinco años.
El informe se produce en un contexto de adopción creciente de estas tecnologías en el ámbito empresarial británico. Según datos de la Oficina de Estadísticas Nacionales (ONS, por sus siglas en inglés), la proporción de empresas que utiliza al menos una tecnología de IA casi se triplicó desde 2023. El gobierno británico, por su parte, proyecta que la adopción de IA podría impulsar la economía hasta en 400.000 millones de libras esterlinas para 2030.
La falta de políticas claras alimenta la desconfianza
Heather Haseley, directora de Aprendizaje Permanente de Imperial Lifelong Learning, señaló que, pese a la rápida adopción de estas herramientas, existe el riesgo de que las habilidades de la fuerza laboral queden rezagadas respecto a lo que la IA puede lograr. “Las habilidades profesionales tienen ahora una vida útil de alrededor de cinco años, menos en el caso de las habilidades técnicas”, afirmó Haseley, citada en el informe.
La directiva atribuyó parte de la inquietud detectada a la ausencia de políticas activas de IA en algunas organizaciones. “Nuestros hallazgos apuntan a cierta inquietud entre los trabajadores del Reino Unido sobre el uso de la IA y su impacto en la economía”, indicó Haseley, quien añadió que la educación tiene un papel central para que las personas de todas las generaciones puedan usar estas herramientas de forma responsable y transparente.
Según Haseley, el respaldo a los empleados más jóvenes debe comenzar antes de que ingresen al mercado laboral. “Los líderes de la industria que entrevistamos para esta investigación señalaron una desconexión entre las actitudes hacia la IA en el ámbito laboral y en el educativo, donde los jóvenes estudiantes pueden ser penalizados por usar estas herramientas, lo que genera una incertidumbre que los acompaña al entrar al mundo laboral”, explicó. Para Haseley, la educación superior debe actuar como puente entre ambos contextos.

articles.title: Watch SpaceX successfully execute the first ‘chopstick’ catch of Starship
articles.text:
After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15’s booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its “Mechazilla” launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed ‘chopstick’ catches of its boosters before, but this is the first time the maneuver has successfully been executed on the Starship vehicle itself.
Watch SpaceX successfully execute the first ‘chopstick’ catch of Starship
SpaceX captured Starship using the arms of ‘Mechazilla’ its launch and catch tower for the first time.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that “success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” While not a complete success, in that the company was unable to recover the entire launch vehicle, it still stands as a milestone for the Starship program. And, since it has previously caught boosters on previous launches, there is reason to believe the failure today was not an insurmountable obstacle. SpaceX is still trying to determine what caused the booster to abort its landing and detonate over the Gulf of Mexico.
In the video above, you can watch Starship plunge through the clouds, flip vertically, and, with surprising grace, ease itself between the waiting arms of Mechazilla at around 4:20 PM ET.

articles.title: WhatsApp-Update: So sieht deine Kontaktliste bald aus
articles.text:
WhatsApp ändert die Kontaktliste: Was du dazu wissen musst
Whatsapp testet für Android-Nutzer:innen eine neue Navigationsleiste, die den „Communities“-Reiter ersetzen soll. In dieser sehen sie, welche ihrer Kontakte derzeit online sind. Außerdem haben Nutzer:innen hier die Möglichkeit, ihre Kontaktliste zu verwalten und Favorit:innen festzulegen. So finden sie aktive Personen schneller, ohne lange durch die Chats scrollen zu müssen. WAbetainfo hat die Neuerung in der Version 2.26.45.2 für Android entdeckt, die im Google Play Store verfügbar ist.
So funktioniert die neue Kontaktliste
Whatsapp ist der beliebteste Messenger der Deutschen. Laut einer Statista-Umfrage kennen ihn hierzulande fast alle und mehr als acht von zehn Erwachsenen nutzen ihn, um mit Kolleg:innen, Freund:innen oder Verwandten in Kontakt zu bleiben. Um die App noch praktischer zu machen, ergänzt der Meta-Dienst regelmäßig neue Reiter und Funktionen. Kürzlich wurde etwa eine Planungsoption vorgestellt, die es ermöglicht, den Versand von Nachrichten bis zu zwei Wochen im Voraus festzulegen. Auch Events sollen Nutzer:innen künftig komplett im Messenger organisieren können – einschließlich Einladungen an Kontakte, die Whatsapp selbst nicht verwenden.
Wie WAbetainfo berichtet, will die App jetzt offenbar auch die Kontakte neu organisieren. Der neue Reiter soll die Personen anzeigen, die Nutzer:innen als Favorit:innen markiert haben. Die Liste lässt sich nach alphabetischer Reihenfolge, Geburtstagen oder Aktivität sortieren. Bei Letzterem sehen sie oben in der Liste, wer gerade online ist. Die Kontakte sind durch einen grünen Punkt gekennzeichnet. Wer gerade nicht online ist, wird nach dem Zeitpunkt der letzten Sichtbarkeit sortiert. Diese Information erscheint allerdings nur, wenn die jeweilige Person den „Zuletzt gesehen“-Status freigibt.
Whatsapp organisiert die Reiter neu
Laut WAbetainfo arbeitet Whatsapp an verschiedenen Konfigurationen für den Reiter „Kontakte“, die von Meta AI, Status-Updates und Kanälen abhängen. Einige Nutzer:innen haben schon jetzt einen Reiter für Meta AI, der den Reiter „Communities“ ersetzt hat. Für sie könnte Whatsapp die neue Navigationsleiste testen, bei dem der „Kontakte“-Reiter den „Meta AI“-Reiter ersetzt. Alternativ könnte es einen separaten Test geben, bei dem der Reiter „Aktuelles“ verschwindet. Da Whatsapp verschiedene Konfigurationen testet, kann die untere Navigationsleiste je nach Konto unterschiedlich aussehen. In dieser ersten Phase konzentriert sich die App laut WAbetainfo aber auf den Reiter „Communities“.
Der Reiter „Kontakte“ ist für einige Nutzer:innen verfügbar, die das neueste Update aus dem Google Play Store installiert haben. Weil Whatsapp die Funktion schrittweise einführt, können aber noch nicht alle Beta-Tester:innen darauf zugreifen. Ist der Reiter noch nicht verfügbar, wird er voraussichtlich in den kommenden Wochen für weitere Android-Nutzer:innen hinzugefügt. Wann die Funktion für alle startet, hat der Meta-Dienst noch nicht bekannt gegeben. Wie praktisch sie ist, bleibt abzuwarten. Viele Nutzer:innen verwenden Privatsphäreeinstellungen, sodass nicht sichtbar ist, wann sie zuletzt online waren. Dadurch funktionieren einige Funktionen der neuen Kontaktliste nur eingeschränkt.

articles.title: Lawyer upgrades eight-V100 private AI server to run 80% of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 4-bit NVFP4 precision — adds 1TB of RAM, an Nvidia RTX 3090, and fixes crashes caused by a bad PSU
articles.text:
Lawyer upgrades eight-V100 private AI server to run 80% of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 4-bit NVFP4 precision — adds 1TB of RAM, an Nvidia RTX 3090, and fixes crashes caused by a bad PSU
The upgrade costs speed: code output falls to 150–180 tokens per second, from 160–215.
A lawyer with a private AI server built on eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs returned with an update, moving about 80% of its work up from 2-bit to 4-bit NVFP4 precision and bringing in 1TB of RAM and an RTX 3090. The server uses DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with a legal harness, the workflows and checks he wraps around the model, for his law practice. The cost? Performance, with code output dropping from 160–215 to 150–180 tokens per second, although the crashes that hit the new build are gone. The culprit behind the crashes, originally blamed on PCIe, was likely a bad PSU.
Once a random hardware nerd lawyer on Reddit, the lawyer's responses to the original breaking story illuminated his identity. He’s a trial lawyer in Columbia, South Carolina. ProprietaryLegalAI commented on our first story three times, linking to a code repository, site, and LinkedIn that identify him as Nick Mermiges, founder of PLI Labs and proprietarylegal.ai. His other firm, PLI, is a technology consultancy, not a law firm, and now lists private, on-prem LLM serving as a service.
He built the software side with AI, specifically Claude Code, which wrote the kernels and ran the benchmarks with his direction. The Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 models handled the optimizations, custom kernels, and re-quantizing; he noted he was surprised at how well Fable built custom Volta kernels, and how it re-quantizes the experts his legal harness triggers. From about February to July, he built a legal harness around Claude that worked, while his attempts at a local-model version failed, but then DeepSeek V4.1 Flash arrived, and he was able to port it successfully, even if he says it’s not as good as frontier.
He reaffirms that “the documents never leave the office” and upgraded the system from 256GB to 1TB of RAM and tossed in a newer GPU, even as the V100s stay on “borrowed time” with R580, the last Nvidia driver branch to support them. The project’s intentions, as listed last time, suggested he wanted the system to be able to offload more of his workload, so this and the precision change are a reasonable upgrade. His previously stated goal of wanting the system to handle more than one request at a time has also been met.
The original “Volta sPLIt” build we covered has transformed into the “Volta Max uPLIft,” still with the clever lettering as his company’s initials are PLI — Proprietary Legal Intelligence. He now claims “near-NVFP4 precision,” having described NVFP4 on our forum earlier this week as “essentially full precision.” NVFP4 is Nvidia’s 4-bit floating-point format, and Nvidia publishes its own NVFP4 version of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; the project’s README says that version matches the precision of the model’s official weights at 4.25 bits per weight.
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is built from “experts,” the parts of the model that do most of the work for each word. This model didn’t fit at that precision before, as 384 routed experts, in each of 40 layers, counts to 15,360 in all. At official precision, this comes out to about 269 GiB, by his estimate, and eight 32GB V100s have 256 GiB in total before anything else is loaded. With the 2-bit build, the weights were 248.8GB; the new build’s Hugging Face package is about 556GB.
The workaround is to keep every expert on the cards at 2-bit and swap the most-used ones up until the cards are full, which in this case came out to about 38.7%, or 5,949 experts, at precisely NVFP4. “Most-used,” in this context, refers to a count from a mix of four kinds of text, which are weighted equally, one of which is his own legal harness traffic.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The payoff is that those experts do most of the work. In testing with one request at a time, between 80% and 86% of decode routes, the calls to an expert made while the model writes, land on the NVFP4 experts, lowest for general text and highest for source code. The prediction for the two-request setup he runs is 78% to 85%. The remaining 15% to 22% of calls would still go to a 2-bit expert.
Measured against Nvidia’s own version of the model as the reference, he was able to get good results. Same next token, or how often a build picks the same next token as the reference, went up to 95.1% from 92.2%. For KL divergence, which measures how far a build’s probabilities are from the reference’s, it went down to 0.079 nats from 0.196. In measuring multiple-choice answers that change, across 513 questions from a standard multiple-choice knowledge test, it went from 79 different to just 8.
This does not measure accuracy — which was about the same across all three cases — but fidelity. Those tests ran on the build’s first release, but not on the new two-request setup he now runs.
The result of the changes: higher fidelity but at a lower level of performance. Code output is 3% to 30% slower, depending on the prompt length, and legal writing is 9% to 23% slower. Before the build, he hoped to maintain about 80 tokens per second on legal and prose; the bench came in at 86 to 106 for legal and 78 to 86 for prose. The upside is that running two requests at once raises total output to 159.0 tokens per second, versus 118.9 with a sole request. The first token also arrives sooner at every prompt length, 108.4 seconds versus 118.7 seconds at 256K tokens.
Each request needs a “slot,” though, and this comes at a cost. Every slot keeps its own state on the cards, which leaves room for fewer NVFP4 experts: 6,215, 5,949, 5,663 for one, two, and three slots, respectively. This means each added slot may push another one to two points of the calls back to 2-bit, which could reduce output quality.
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on eight Tesla V100s: 2-bit vs. near-NVFP4 build, by prompt length |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Prompt length | Wait for first token, 2-bit / near-NVFP4 | Code (tokens/s), 2-bit / near-NVFP4 | Legal writing (tokens/s), 2-bit / near-NVFP4 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 1K tokens | 1.2 / 1.0 seconds | 215.0 / 150.1 | 117.6 / 105.5 | 
| 32K tokens | 17.2 / 16.0 seconds | 200.5 / 165.1 | 116.5 / 93.4 | 
| 128K tokens | 59.2 / 54.3 seconds | 182.8 / 151.4 | 110.9 / 87.3 | 
| 256K tokens | 118.7 / 108.4 seconds | 160.0 / 154.6 | 103.1 / 93.5 | 
Builder’s measurements, Nov. 5 (2-bit) and Nov. 12 (near-NVFP4); greedy decoding, thinking off, one request at a time.
The move to more RAM came this week with eight 128GB modules at 2,933 MT/s, originally eight 32GB modules that had to be run at DDR4-2666 due to ECC errors. After the RAM upgrade, the host reports two NUMA nodes, and two boots hung at the first transfer between the boards, so he reordered the cards in software. The GPUs remain capped at 1,522 MHz, as before.
As for the PSU, he took the common approach of chasing PCIe slots, cards, and cables to narrow down the cause, finally concluding it was “probably one bad PSU.” He also added more fans, but with no temperature changes, this only indicated that airflow was not the problem. He changed the power delivery, and nine of nine long chats read clean afterward. Also, don’t judge his cable management skill; any “advice [there] is welcome and will be ignored,” which is the only comment to make in that situation.
He also already has two DGX Sparks running the same model at 1M context for agent work, and three or four sessions at once, and he isn’t stopping there. Now it comes down to scaling. Eight more V100s and a second server, with 512GB of 3,200 MT/s ECC RAM, are waiting in the wings. The second box would run another high-precision DeepSeek, used as an extra agent or to run tasks in parallel. The plan is also to move DeepSeek’s small draft model off the V100s and onto the RTX 3090, which hasn’t happened yet.

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering is getting a Netflix animated series. For real this time.
articles.text:
“It’s really happening. I promise. For real.” Those are the first words from Roy Graham, Head of Story at Magic: The Gathering, in a video posted yesterday announcing Planeswalker, the animated series heading to Netflix in 2027.
Magic: The Gathering is getting a Netflix animated series. For real this time.
Magic The Gathering: Planeswalker is set to debut on Netflix in 2027.
An animated Magic: The Gathering series was first teased back in 2019 with Joe and Anthony Russo at the helm. But that fell apart. In 2024, Netflix announced it still planned to make a series based on the game, but it decided to rework it from the ground up.
Now fans are finally getting their first glimpse of the show, which will be called Planeswalker. According to the sneak peek, because each plane exists in its own pocket universe, it will have a unique design, animation, and filmmaking style.
According to a synopsis of the show shared with IGN, Planeswalker will focus on Chandra Nalaar, a “volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past.” Storyline details beyond that are vague, other than mentioning an “insidious force” that Chandra and other Planeswalkers will team up to confront “to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence.”

articles.title: Nvidia deliberately kept GPU prices high through circular financing deals, report claims
articles.text:
Connecting the dots: The AI boom has been widely blamed for GPU prices spinning out of control over the past year. Following Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia,new information suggests that this was the goal of the former CEO's business strategy, which has long drawn accusations of circular financing.
A recent Wall Street Journal profile of Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress has shed more light on how Nvidia controversially financed its own customers to drive the AI boom. According to the report, the company pushed for more deals in mid-to-late 2026 to absorb an oversupply of TSMC wafers and keep GPU prices high.
Since at least last year, Nvidia has been accused of prolonging the AI boom by supporting the companies that buy its chips. Co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, along with CFO Kress, even went so far as to defend the company against comparisons to Enron, which used similar tactics to illegally obscure its debt before its 2001 collapse.
Also read: GPU Prices Are Spiraling Out of Control - Q4 2026 Update
Behind the scenes, Kress expressed concern about the scale of the deals Nvidia had inked with cloud providers and major AI companies like OpenAI. Nvidia pushed ahead anyway, but by summer 2026, the company was wondering whether it had pushed too far amid an "avalanche" of semiconductors it had ordered from TSMC.
It was around this time that Huang berated Kress, calling her "a deer in headlights," according to someone familiar with the matter. Nvidia began to slow down, downsize, and pause some of its financing deals, including one with OpenAI that originally included a $250 billion backstop for the world's largest data center.
AI data centers have siphoned off DRAM and NAND manufacturing capacity traditionally used for RAM and storage in consumer devices, inflating prices. Nvidia's GeForce GPUs have been hit especially hard, with prices often exceeding 160% of their original MSRP. The company's flagship RTX 5090 has become unobtainable because Nvidia has directed its VRAM and semiconductors toward data center GPUs.
Related: Without Jensen Huang, is it game over for GeForce?
As its financial support deals wound down, Huang became worried about the company's stock market valuation, with its average monthly stock multiple falling far behind those of other large tech companies.
At a Berlin conference, the former CEO told major clients a story about a busy Japanese soup vendor who refused to give him a second serving after he had waited in a long line, saying the vendor had too many customers and not enough soup. Huang used the story to highlight the value of maintaining a diverse customer base and keeping prices high, suggesting that Nvidia's circular financing strategy inflated GPU prices by creating the perception of high demand.
The story emerged after Huang's resignation following the revelation of multiple extramarital affairs. One was with Alice Huang (no relation), whose company, Megaspeed, was suspected by US intelligence of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of export regulations. While some allege that she is a spy for Beijing, President Trump and the Justice Department said that hasn't been determined.

articles.title: R$ 34 bilhões: Binance cobriu prejuízo do maior roubo de cripto da história • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
R$ 34 bilhões: Binance cobriu prejuízo do maior roubo de cripto da história
Corretora de criptomoedas anunciou aos clientes que cobriu os ativos que foram roubados em ataque hacker no final de outubro.
A corretora Binance disse que cobriu 100% dos US$ 6,3 bilhões (R$ 34 bilhões, em conversão direta) que haviam sido roubados no ataque hacker de 29 de outubro. A empresa anunciou a normalização em um post no X. Além disso, também foi publicada uma nova Prova de Reserva indicando a reposição dos criptoativos nas carteiras dos clientes afetados.
Apesar da cobertura integral do roubo, a reposição não significa recuperação: os bilhões de dólares roubados em criptomoedas ainda não voltaram para a empresa. Segundo o site Quartz, a Binance combinou recursos do seu fundo de emergência com a compra de novos tokens e outras fontes para chegar aos 100% do valor roubado.
Esse pode ter sido o maior roubo a criptoativos já registrado. A maior parte do montante foi transferida em apenas 20 minutos. Segundo investigação feita pela TRM Labs, empresa de inteligência em blockchain e cripto, os responsáveis fazem parte do grupo TraderTraitor, supostamente ligado ao governo da Coréia do Norte. O país nega qualquer relação com o ataque.
Uma parte relevante do recurso roubado foi reposta dois dias após as transações fraudulentas. A Binance anunciou em 31 de outubro que havia combinado diferentes fundos para chegar ao montante de US$ 6 bilhões. Entre as fontes estão o seu fundo de emergência SAFU, seu fundo de garantia e também a partir de sua tesouraria corporativa.
Nas últimas semanas, a empresa conseguiu os últimos 10% por meio da compra de tokens, tanto na bolsa de cripto quanto via OTC (over-the-counter, ou mercado de balcão), em negociação direta.
Desde que a situação foi divulgada, a Binance assumiu todos os custos. Até o momento, a empresa não revelou se conseguiu recuperar alguma parte das ações roubadas, mas garantiu que não iria repassar as perdas para os clientes.
O roubo teria sido realizado por meio do acesso indevido ao computador de um engenheiro de DevOps (setor de desenvolvimento e operações). Uma vez com as credenciais da vítima, os cibercriminosos fizeram diversas transferências autorizadas internamente, sem a necessidade de burlar a segurança para enviar as ações. Segundo a Binance, essa não foi a única vulnerabilidade no caso, e a solução imediata foi bloquear todas as movimentações pela plataforma. O sistema só foi retomado no dia 3 de novembro.
Segundo relatório da TRM Labs, os hackers transformaram um pool de liquidez em uma rota de lavagem de dinheiro. Basicamente, esses ativos foram transferidos e trocados por criptomoedas recém cunhadas pelos próprios criminosos. O valor foi convertido em dólares e, depois, reconvertidos em cripto, utilizando moedas como Ethereum (ETH) e Bitcoins (BTC). Isso aconteceu em diversas carteiras, dificultando o rastreio por completo.

articles.title: China’s Air Force builds drone that shoots painkiller darts at wounded soldiers — experimental PLA UAV injects emergency meds from a distance to keep medics out of danger and buys time during the 'Golden Hour'
articles.text:
China’s Air Force builds drone that shoots painkiller darts at wounded soldiers — experimental PLA UAV injects emergency meds from a distance to keep medics out of danger and buys time during the 'Golden Hour'
This won't magically bring units to 100% health, but it should increase survival rates for wounded soldiers in the frontlines.
A Chinese military medical school has just developed a UAV that could remotely administer medicine, helping treat injured soldiers on the front lines without putting medical personnel at risk. According to Chinese mouthpiece Global Times, the Air Force Medical University built the first casualty-search drone for the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) that fires darts loaded with painkillers to help ease the pain of wounded personnel.
“We have developed the military’s first casualty-search drone and have also made some breakthroughs in treatment. For example, we can use drones to inject medication into wounded personnel from a considerable distance,” Air Force Medical University representative Wang Jianqi told the publication. “Wherever our drone can fly, we can deliver life-saving emergency medication into a wounded person’s muscle, buying valuable time for treatment.”
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine saw the widespread use of drones on the frontline, primarily for search-and-destroy and reconnaissance missions. However, the four-year escalation of the 12-year war has seen the creative implementations of these units — from jam-proof fiber optic drones to the use of heavy-lift hexacopters for medical evacuation. Now, drones-as-first-responders are being developed for civilian use, including firefighting drones, camera response drones, and even “Campus Guardian Angel” drones designed to neutralize school shooters.
However, China's air-ground treatment drone remains in the experimental stage, says Wang. After all, you can’t just administer medication without assessing the patient’s vital signs and their injuries. It’s also difficult or even impossible to load an incapacitated soldier without external assistance. Still, the deployment of medical UAVs would help with battlefield medicine, which has developed the concept of the “golden hour,” which suggests that wounded personnel treated within the first hour have the greatest chance of survival.
Although battlefield medicine was in use since the 1800s, especially during Napoleon’s invasion of Russia and the American Civil War, helicopter medevacs were first deployed during World War 2 in Burma and the Philippines. The Korean War saw the introduction of MASH — Mobile Army Surgical Hospital — units that brought forward treatment units closer to the frontline.
This, combined with the widespread use of UH-1 Hueys during the Vietnam War to evacuate wounded soldiers from the front lines, sometimes while under enemy fire, has greatly increased the survival rate among wounded soldiers. Today, helicopter and ground medevacs are common among military forces, with drone treatment and evacuation now being experimented with in both the frontlines of Ukraine and military medical universities in China.

articles.title: Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer
articles.text:
Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer
AI agents have had a URL problem for a while. When an agent needs current information but has no search tool, it often makes up the web address it thinks the answer lives at. It might guess something like docs.example.com/v4.2/auth, try to load it, and get a “page not found” error because the page doesn’t exist. Then it either keeps guessing or falls back on outdated information from its training.
“Live web search gives AI agents fresh pages. Deciding which ones to trust over your own data is still a ranking problem.”
Infrastructure providers have noticed. In October, InfoQ reported that Cloudflare opened a beta Web Search API in its AI Gateway. Agents can call several search providers through one interface and get live results back with source links, logging, and access controls attached. Cloudflare’s reasoning was refreshingly direct: Without search, agents tend to guess.
This is a welcome change, and live search will probably be a default agent tool within a year, but it solves only the finding part of the problem. Once fresh pages are in front of an agent, something still has to decide which of those pages, and which of your own documents, the agent should actually rely on. That decision lives in your retrieval layer.
The problem: two pools of evidence, one context window
An agent working inside a company rarely answers from the web alone. It also has the data that makes it useful to that company: product catalogs, documentation, contracts, support history, account records,s and permissions. With web search wired in, every step of a task can now pull from two very different pools.
|  | Web results | Internal data | 
| Freshness | Often hours or days old | Can be months out of date without anyone noticing | 
| Quality | Uneven: official docs next to forum threads | Curated, but written for a past state of the product | 
| Structure | Mostly unstructured text | Mix of text, metadata and structured records | 
| Authority | Has to be inferred from the source | Known, but rarely stored as a field | 
| Access control | Public | Per customer, region, contract or role | 
The agent has to reconcile these, often several times within one task. And the questions it needs answered are ones a search API was never built to handle. When yesterday’s vendor changelog contradicts an internal knowledge base article from last spring, which one wins? Does this result apply to this customer’s version and region? Is the agent even allowed to show it?
Those are ranking and filtering decisions. They depend on your data and business rules, so you have to make them where both are available.
Why concatenating results breaks in production
The simplest integration is to run a web search, run an internal search, append one list to the other, and let the model sort it out. It may work well at first, but once it’s running against growing data and traffic, it tends to fail in a few predictable ways:
- Conflicts go unresolved. The model sees two confident sources that disagree and has no signal for which is newer or more authoritative, so it picks one or blends them into an answer that matches neither.
- Staleness hides. A 3-month-old knowledge base article that matches the user’s wording almost exactly will beat a 4-day-old changelog on similarity alone. Nothing in the embedding says the article is out of date.
- Permissions are applied too late. If access rules run after retrieval, restricted content may already be in the prompt. If they run crudely, useful results get dropped along with sensitive ones.
- Cost and latency compound. A person runs one search and reads the results. An agent can trigger a dozen or more retrieval calls in a single task as it plans, checks, and refines. Sending every candidate to the model on every call adds up quickly, and more context doesn’t reliably produce better answers.
A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does.
“A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does.”
Clarm, a Y Combinator company that builds sales and support agents for open-source software companies, hit this early. Its founder, Marcus Storm-Mollard, said the team realized “search, not generation, was the real problem to solve.” Generating an answer was the easy part. Finding the right information to ground it in was the hard part, which is why Clarm runs text search, vector similarity, and structured filters through a single query instead of stitching separate stores together.
What changes when agents search across sources
When agents combine live web results with internal data, they need to account for different retrieval methods, metadata, permissions, and ranking signals. Four design considerations stand out.
1. Retrieve across methods in one query
Keyword matching catches exact product names, error codes, and version strings, which embeddings are notoriously bad at. Vector search catches paraphrases and intent. Structured filters enforce hard constraints like customer, version, and entitlement.
Within a single indexed collection, hybrid retrieval can combine keyword matching, vector similarity, and structured filters. That does not, by itself, fuse results from an external web search API with results from an internal index. The two-source integration requires a separate design decision.
select * from evidence where
  ({targetHits: 200}nearestNeighbor(embedding, q) or userQuery())
  and visibility contains "customer"
  and product_version contains "4.2"
The broader lesson is that retrieval systems need to handle lexical matching, semantic similarity, and filtering together. These requirements matter regardless of the search platform chosen. Perplexity hit this wall when it set out to build search in-house for its answer engine. Its CEO, Aravind Srinivas, has summed up the company’s approach as “first solve search, then solve everything else.” But when the team evaluated existing tools, it found that vector databases couldn’t reliably support even simple Boolean filters, while traditional search backends offered only primitive semantic ranking. It needed lexical retrieval, semantic retrieval, and filtering in one engine, at consumer scale, and chose Vespa to build it.
2. Rank on more than similarity
Relevance to the query is only one signal. Agents also need to weigh freshness, source authority, and business rules together: official documentation over forum threads, last week’s changelog over last year’s wiki page, the customer’s contracted version over the latest release.
Multiphase ranking is a practical way to do this. A cheap first phase scores thousands of candidates on a blend of signals, and a more expensive learned model reorders the few that remain:
rank-profile agent_evidence {
    inputs {
        query(q) tensor<float>(x[384])
    }
    rank-properties {
        freshness(published_at).maxAge: 7776000
    }
    first-phase {
        expression: bm25(body) + closeness(field, embedding) + 0.5 * freshness(published_at) + attribute(source_authority)
    }
    second-phase {
        rerank-count: 100
        expression: xgboost("evidence-ranker.json")
    }
}
The important part isn’t the specific weights. It’s that freshness and authority are explicit, inspectable inputs to the score, not something you hope the model infers from the text. (The maxAge setting controls how quickly freshness decays; here it’s 90 days.)
“The important part isn’t the specific weights. It’s that freshness and authority are explicit, inspectable inputs to the score, not something you hope the model infers from the text.”
Metal AI, which builds an intelligence platform for private equity firms, runs into this with due diligence questionnaires. Firms answer thousands of them from investors, and a model can’t freely generate the answers. They have to come from a bank of responses that legal has already approved, and that bank changes over time and lives in documents and spreadsheets. Similarity alone could easily surface an approved answer that’s been replaced. So Metal indexes the answer bank with recency in mind and ranks freshness alongside semantic similarity, so the agent pulls the current approved answer, not just the closest match.
3. Treat web results as candidates, not answers
Web search and internal retrieval often return separate result sets, each with its own relevance signals. Simply passing both sets to the model leaves it to reconcile differences in freshness, authority, and relevance.
A more deliberate approach is to evaluate evidence from both sources against a consistent set of criteria before selecting what goes into the prompt. Vespa’s flexible ranking capabilities can support this approach, but the implementation depends on how the external results are integrated into the retrieval pipeline.
Depending on provider terms and system constraints, teams might index permitted external content into a shared search collection or retrieve from separate systems and apply a subsequent fusion or reranking step. There is no universal fusion method. Each option has trade-offs in latency, freshness, score comparability, and operational complexity.
4. Hold up at agent call volume
This isn’t a hypothetical load pattern. At Metal, AI agents handle 95% of retrieval, not people. When someone asks for a portfolio company’s EBITDA, an agent decides which entity types to query (documents, companies, metrics, activities), applies recency and workflow filters, runs the query, and then keeps going, paginating or pulling related entities until it has enough context to answer. Clarm sees something similar from the other direction: developers working alongside its agents send thousands of queries a day, in sessions that have run as long as 22 hours.
“They need the precision and controls of expert search, delivered with the low latency and high throughput of consumer search.”
Every one of those calls sits on the critical path to the agent’s answer. Retrieval and ranking need to stay predictable under that load, which favors running inference where the data already lives instead of shipping large candidate sets across the network to a separate ranking service. Every network hop you remove is latency you get back on every call, multiplied by every step of the task. Jon Bratseth, Vespa’s CEO, describes this as the central engineering challenge with agents: They need the precision and controls of expert search, delivered with the low latency and high throughput of consumer search.
A worked example: the support agent and the changelog
Here’s a scenario most support teams will recognize. A customer upgrades a payments SDK from 4.1 to 4.2, their checkout integration stops working, and they open a ticket.
The agent does what you’d want and searches the web first. It finds the SDK’s changelog from four days ago, which deprecates the authentication call the integration relies on, and a forum thread where another developer posted a workaround. Then it searches internally, returning a March knowledge base article that still tells customers to use the old call, the customer’s account record showing they’re on 4.2, and a restricted engineering ticket about the same bug.
Handed to the model as one long list, this is a trap. The knowledge base article matches the customer’s wording almost exactly, so it ranks well on similarity. The forum workaround reads confidently. The engineering ticket contains notes the customer should never see.
When the retrieval layer is doing its job, both sets of evidence go through the same pipeline. In this example, the team uses a shared collection: web results are indexed into Vespa as short-lived documents alongside internal data, retrieved with one query and scored by rank profiles aligned with the same business rules:
For this ticket, that means:
- The visibility filter excludes the internal ticket at query time, so it never reaches the prompt.
- The version filter keeps only material that applies to the library version on the customer’s account.
- Ranking boosts the changelog for authority and recency, demotes the older knowledge base article, and keeps the forum thread as supporting evidence.
- The model receives three or four well-ordered passages instead of twenty, each with its source.
In this illustrative outcome, the answer cites the changelog, explains the change, and points to the supported fix. The search API helps find fresh evidence, and the retrieval design determines which evidence the agent receives.
Before you wire web search into an agent
- Store dates and source types on everything. Internal or external, every document needs a publication date and a source type you can rank on.
- Write signals into the documents themselves. Keep freshness, authority, and source type on each document instead of in a separate feature store. That way they shape ranking from the first phase, not just when reranking the top results.
- Always include lexical signals. Even when your embeddings are strong, keyword matching is what catches the exact version numbers, error codes, and product names agents depend on.
- Filter in the query. Apply permissions at retrieval time, not in post-processing.
- Send passages, not pages. Rank the chunks within each retrieved document and pass only the most relevant spans to the model, sized to what it actually needs per call.
- Measure retrieval on its own. Build a test set of real agent questions and track whether the right evidence lands in the top results, separately from how the model phrases the answer.
- Load-test at agent volume. Benchmark with the number of retrieval calls a typical task actually makes, not one query per request.
Final thoughts
Managed web search for agents removes a real, frustrating failure mode, and more teams will adopt it as it leaves beta. That makes the next question more pressing. When an agent can see the open web and your private data at the same time, the quality of its work depends on how well it chooses between them.
Bratseth puts it more simply: Relevance is your moat. As models get more capable and more widely available, most companies end up with access to roughly the same intelligence. What sets them apart is their own information and how well their systems use it. He breaks relevance into four parts: comprehensiveness, freshness, recall accuracy, and ranking quality. Live web search helps with the first two. The last two are still yours to build.
The model shouldn’t improvise that choice on every call. It belongs in a retrieval layer you can inspect, test, and tune, where you weigh freshness, authority, permissions, and relevance together. Web search helps agents find evidence. Ranking is how they decide what to believe.
For teams building agents, the practical next step is to evaluate retrieval quality separately from answer generation: test whether the right evidence appears, whether permissions are enforced before context assembly, and whether fresh and authoritative sources are prioritized when documents conflict.
If you want to try this pattern, Vespa combines lexical, vector, and structured retrieval with multi-phase ranking in one pipeline, and it’s available as open source or as a managed service on Vespa Cloud. The RAG Blueprint walks through how to design the schema, retrieval strategy, and ranking phases step by step, and you can start a free trial to build it yourself.

articles.title: Una fila gigante de tanques Abrams avanza hasta donde alcanza la vista en EEUU. Su destino no es Ucrania, y lo que llega por mar es todavía más inquietante
articles.text:
En una pequeña localidad de Estados Unidos, un tren de mercancías ha convertido una jornada cualquiera en un espectáculo militar. Sobre sus vagones viajaba una interminable fila de algunos de los carros de combate más avanzados del planeta. Su destino no es Ucrania, sino un país que está reconstruyendo su ejército a una velocidad que empieza a sorprender incluso a los ucranianos.
Un tren que no parece tener fin. El pasado 1 de noviembre, los habitantes de La Grange, una localidad de unos 10.000 habitantes en Kentucky cuya línea ferroviaria atraviesa el centro urbano, asistieron al paso de un convoy militar extraordinario. Sobre sus vagones viajaban 33 carros de combate Abrams M1A2 SEPv3, identificados posteriormente por periodistas y analistas de inteligencia de fuentes abiertas.
Las imágenes se propagaron rápidamente por las redes sociales, pero lo más interesante no era el tamaño del convoy, sino su destino: Polonia, que comparte frontera con Rusia a través del enclave de Kaliningrado.
Los últimos 33 de un ejército formidable. La cifra de carros que aparece en el vídeo no parece casual. El 5 de abril de 2022, apenas unas semanas después de la invasión rusa de Ucrania, Polonia firmó un contrato de 4.750 millones de dólares para adquirir 250 Abrams M1A2 SEPv3, junto con un amplio paquete de formación, logística y asistencia técnica.
Las entregas comenzaron en enero de 2025 y, en septiembre de 2026, el Ministerio de Defensa polaco confirmó que ya disponía de 217 unidades. Los 33 carros filmados en Kentucky coinciden exactamente con los que faltan para completar el pedido, cuya entrega está prevista antes de finalizar el año.
Lo mejor del arsenal estadounidense. No estamos hablando de vehículos antiguos rescatados de algún almacén militar. Los M1A2 SEPv3 constituyen la versión más avanzada del Abrams actualmente en servicio en el Ejército estadounidense, con sistemas modernizados de observación, comunicaciones y control de tiro.
Su armamento principal es un cañón de ánima lisa M256 de 120 milímetros, capaz de atacar objetivos blindados a distancias superiores a los tres kilómetros, y cuentan con una turbina de gas de unos 1.500 caballos. Además, Polonia ya recibió entre 2023 y 2024 otros 116 Abrams M1A1FEP, lo que elevará su flota de carros estadounidenses a 366 unidades.
Y entonces llegaron los barcos. Mientras las imágenes del tren de Kentucky circulaban por Internet, Polonia acababa de recibir el último cargamento de armamento pesado surcoreano de 2026. Lo contamos. A bordo viajaban varias decenas de carros K2 Black Panther y obuses autopropulsados K9 Thunder, aunque las autoridades no han precisado el número exacto.
El envío forma parte de una operación todavía más ambiciosa: Varsovia ha contratado 360 carros K2 y 364 obuses K9 de 155 milímetros. En agosto de 2025 firmó un segundo contrato para adquirir 180 K2 por unos 6.500 millones de dólares, mientras que el último gran pedido de artillería, firmado en diciembre de 2023, ascendió a otros 2.600 millones.
Una fábrica de tanques en Europa. Lo que diferencia la operación surcoreana de una simple compra de armamento es que Polonia quiere fabricar sus propios carros. El acuerdo marco firmado con Hyundai Rotem en 2022 contempla la adquisición de hasta 1.000 K2, aunque por ahora solo se han contratado formalmente 360. El segundo pedido incluye 64 unidades de la variante mejorada K2PL, de las cuales 61 se producirán en las instalaciones polacas de Bumar-Łabędy entre 2028 y 2030.
Varsovia también está desarrollando su capacidad para mantener los Abrams, con unas nuevas instalaciones de reparación terminadas en Poznań en 2026. El objetivo es reducir la dependencia exterior y garantizar que semejante arsenal pueda mantenerse operativo durante décadas.
Un movimiento que no ha pasado desapercibido en Ucrania. Los analistas ucranianos han destacado tanto la velocidad del rearme polaco como el destino de las últimas entregas surcoreanas. Los nuevos K2 y K9 irán a dos brigadas de la 16ª División Mecanizada de Pomerania, desplegada en el noreste del país y responsable de defender regiones próximas a Rusia y Bielorrusia.
Se trata, qué duda cabe, de una zona especialmente delicada para la OTAN, situada cerca del corredor de Suwałki, la estrecha franja de territorio que conecta Polonia con Lituania y separa Kaliningrado de Bielorrusia. En otras palabras, parte de ese enorme arsenal está siendo destinado precisamente a uno de los puntos más vulnerables de la alianza.
La paradoja de Putin. Desde el comienzo de la invasión rusa, Polonia ha entregado a Ucrania numerosos carros T-72 y PT-91 de origen soviético, además de sistemas de artillería. Sin embargo, lejos de debilitar permanentemente su ejército, esas donaciones han acelerado una transformación extraordinaria. Entre los Abrams estadounidenses y los K2 surcoreanos, Varsovia ha contratado ya 726 carros de combate, sin contar los Leopard 2 alemanes que también forman parte de su arsenal.
La invasión que pretendía consolidar la influencia rusa sobre su entorno ha terminado impulsando la construcción de una de las mayores fuerzas acorazadas de Europa justo al otro lado de sus fronteras. Y el interminable tren que atravesó Kentucky es apenas una pequeña muestra de ello.

articles.title: Irene Gramage, abogada, acerca de los repartos de bienes: “Heredar no es gratis, cuesta dinero. No solo está el impuesto de sucesiones, también la plusvalía municipal”
articles.text:
Incluso aunque tengamos en cuenta que el impuesto a pagar sea pequeño, no son gratuitas todas estas transmisiones de los padres a los hijos. La abogada Irene Gramage advierte de esa confusión: “Heredar no es gratis, cuesta dinero. No solo está el impuesto de sucesiones, también la plusvalía municipal”, explica la abogada Irene Gramage.
Por otra parte, las comunidades autónomas pueden establecer ciertas ventajas fiscales. De esta forma pueden reducir notablemente la cuota que se debe pagar en el impuesto de sucesiones (sobre todo entre familiares directos). Es importante saber qué beneficios están asociados a la sucesión de unos padres a unos hijos y qué requisitos deben cumplirse según los bienes que se adquieren.
También es relevante conocer a qué comunidad autónoma nos estamos refiriendo. En el caso de las sucesiones sometidas al régimen común (con el causante y los herederos residentes en España), el lugar de residencia habitual es el lugar de residencia habitual del fallecido (no del heredero). De acuerdo con la Ley 22/2009, el sitio de residencia habitual es aquel donde el causante haya estado mayor número de días en los cinco años anteriores al devengo.
Gastos que están fuera de Sucesiones
En primer lugar, no siempre es suficiente con realizar una liquidación con un importe pequeño (o nulo) en el impuesto. Por ejemplo, en el caso de que los bienes sean objeto de una escritura notarial y se inscriban en el Registro de la Propiedad, va a haber unos gastos asociados a los servicios notariales. Además, los servicios notariales no están exentos de honorarios por el hecho de que se aplique una bonificación en sucesiones. No todas las herencias tienen los mismos procedimientos.
El Consejo General del Notariado explica que los servicios notariales están sujetos a un arancel. Por otro lado están los gastos de inscripción de inmuebles. Estos tienen los costes que establece el arancel de los registradores.
También hay que matizar respecto al tema de la plusvalía municipal. Los terrenos urbanos contenidos en la herencia pueden estar sujetos a este impuesto. Pero no es algo que se pague de manera automática por recibir cualquier bien. El artículo 104 de la Ley de Haciendas Locales establece que están excluidos los terrenos rústicos. También están excluidos aquellos casos en los que se demuestre que no ha habido incremento del valor del suelo.
Como señala Gramage, es importante saber cuál es el coste real y fundamental distinguir entre la liquidación de sucesiones y otros gastos. Los aspectos fiscales relacionados con las transmisiones familiares están relacionados con las características de la operación.

articles.title: Cet appareil peut nettoyer et sécher canapés et tapis
articles.text:
Tineco Carpet One Spot DualHeat : un coup de chaud sur les taches du canapé et des tapis
Les taches sous pression
Eau chaude, vapeur et séchage à air chaud : le Carpet One Spot DualHeat multiplie les moyens de détacher les textiles. Tineco lance ce nettoyeur à 249 €, avec une offre Black Friday à 209,99 € jusqu'au 30 novembre.
Un café renversé sur le canapé, des traces de pattes sur le tapis... Tineco s'attaque aux accidents domestiques avec le Carpet One Spot DualHeat. Ce nettoyeur pour textiles associe projection d'eau chaude ou de vapeur et aspiration des saletés. Il vise aussi bien les tissus d'ameublement que les matelas, paniers pour animaux ou encore sièges de voiture.
Le système DualHeat propose de l'eau chauffée à 70 °C ou de la vapeur à 100 °C. L'eau chaude doit aider à décoller les salissures courantes et grasses, tandis que la vapeur cible les résidus incrustés. La dépression atteint 17 kPa pour aspirer l'eau et les saletés.
Quatre modes couvrent le nettoyage : Cool Clean pour les taches fraîches, Warm Clean à l'eau chaude, Steam Clean à la vapeur et Boost Steam pour renforcer cette dernière.
Un canapé au sec ?
L'originalité se trouve aussi dans le séchage. Gr^ce au système baptisé FlipDry, une plaque ajustable dirige de l'air chaud vers la zone nettoyée. Tineco annonce une température de 70 °C max et deux réglages plus ou moins chaud selon la fragilité du textile. Le fabricant évoque un séchage en seulement trois minutes sans indiquer la surface ni les conditions de cette mesure.
L'appareil embarque un réservoir d'eau propre de 1,2 l et un bac d'eau sale de 0,9 l. Une brosse pour tissus, un embout pour les recoins et un accessoire de nettoyage du tuyau complètent l'ensemble. Une raclette étend les usages aux vitres, miroirs et surfaces de salle de bain.
Disponible chez Tineco et sur Amazon au prix conseillé de 249 €, le Carpet One Spot DualHeat est proposé à 209,99 € pour le Black Friday jusqu'au 30 novembre 2026.

articles.title: Les cartes GeForce menacées par le départ de Jensen Huang ? La réponse très sèche de Nvidia aux joueurs — Frandroid
articles.text:
Cette semaine, Jacob Freeman était à la PDXLAN, l’une des plus grandes LAN parties d’Amérique du Nord, où Nvidia tient un stand depuis des années.
L’évangéliste GeForce de Nvidia, chargé du lien avec les joueurs, la presse et les créateurs de contenu, y a publié des photos accompagnées d’un message sur X : beaucoup de choses se sont passées cette semaine, mais le travail des équipes qui aiment le jeu PC continue. Un internaute lui a alors demandé ce qu’il pensait des commentaires annonçant la fin de GeForce. Sa réponse tient en un mot, « Nope », accompagné d’un émoji.
Ce message arrive deux jours après la démission de Jensen Huang, qui a ravivé les craintes des joueurs. Le fondateur de Nvidia était le principal défenseur d’une activité jeu vidéo devenue marginale dans les comptes, puisque les GeForce sont désormais noyées dans une catégorie « Edge Computing » qui pesait à peine 7,5 % du chiffre d’affaires au dernier trimestre.
Jouez dans les meilleures conditions avec la TV TCL P89L : une expérience gaming fluide en 144 Hz et 4K , actuellement en promotion !
Comme nous l’expliquions dans notre analyse sur l’avenir des GeForce RTX, le risque était surtout celui d’une lente relégation, avec moins de lancements et des prix dictés par la mémoire disponible.
    Pour aller plus loin
Joueurs PC, mauvaise nouvelle : le dernier défenseur des GeForce RTX a quitté Nvidia
            
Un démenti utile mais qui reste limité
Le message a le mérite d’être clair, et il émane bien de Nvidia. Jacob Freeman, ancien responsable produit chez EVGA, occupe toutefois un poste de relations avec la communauté, loin des arbitrages budgétaires de la direction.
Un « Nope » sur X ne dit rien du calendrier des prochaines cartes, des volumes de production ou des prix, alors qu’aucune nouvelle génération de GeForce n’est sortie cette année.
Sur ce dernier point, la situation reste tendue, puisque la RTX 5090 revient en stock chez certains revendeurs américains à environ trois fois son prix de lancement.
    Pour aller plus loin
RTX 5090 : pourquoi vous aurez un mal fou à en acheter une en 2027
            
Personne ne prédisait sérieusement une disparition brutale de GeForce, qui reste la porte d’entrée de CUDA pour des millions de développeurs et partage l’essentiel de son architecture avec les puces pour data centers. La vraie question porte sur la priorité que la nouvelle direction accordera aux joueurs face aux clients de l’IA, qui se disputent la même mémoire et les mêmes capacités de production.
Le vrai test, le 17 novembre
La première réponse officielle viendra de Colette Kress, la directrice financière devenue patronne par intérim, lors de la publication des résultats trimestriels le 17 novembre. Le précédent rapport ne mentionnait ni GeForce ni le jeu vidéo : un mot sur les joueurs, même bref, serait bienvenu.
    Pour aller plus loin
Qui est Colette Kress, la financière qui prend les commandes de Nvidia après Jensen Huang ?
            
Nvidia a eu raison de couper court aux rumeurs les plus alarmistes, et GeForce ne va pas disparaître du jour au lendemain.
Mais un évangéliste ne fixe ni les budgets ni les priorités, surtout dans une entreprise qui cherche encore son patron depuis le départ de Jensen Huang. Pour les joueurs, le signal à guetter viendra de la direction, et la menace d’une relégation des GeForce RTX au second rang n’a pas disparu avec ce « Nope ».
    Pour aller plus loin
Nvidia officialise le départ de Jensen Huang et confie les clés à sa directrice financière

articles.title: Office sans abonnement sur Mac : le bon choix dépend d’abord de votre version de macOS
articles.text:
Vous souhaitez utiliser Word, Excel et PowerPoint sur votre Mac sans souscrire à un abonnement Microsoft 365 ? Plusieurs versions d'Office existent, mais toutes ne sont pas compatibles avec les mêmes systèmes. Avant de choisir votre licence, un premier réflexe s'impose, à savoir vérifier la version de macOS installée sur votre ordinateur.
Word, Excel et PowerPoint. Une triplette de logiciels dont il est parfois bien difficile de se passer, que ce soit pour travailler, étudier ou gérer ses documents au quotidien. Pourtant, tout le monde n'a pas nécessairement envie de payer un abonnement (via Microsoft 365) pour accéder à ces applications. Microsoft propose toujours des versions d'Office à l'achat unique, notamment Office 2024 et Office 2021 pour Mac. Une solution intéressante… à condition de choisir la bonne édition. Car sur un ordinateur Apple, la compatibilité dépend avant tout de la version de macOS utilisée.
Microsoft 365 ou Office pour Mac sans abonnement : quelle formule choisir ?
Avant même de s’intéresser aux différentes licences, il faut distinguer deux approches. D'un côté, Microsoft 365 fonctionne sur abonnement et donne accès aux applications Office, avec des mises à jour régulières et des fonctionnalités qui évoluent au fil du temps. C'est une formule adaptée à ceux qui souhaitent toujours disposer des dernières nouveautés et qui utilisent également les services connectés de Microsoft.
De l'autre, les versions d'Office qui reposent sur un achat unique. Une fois la licence acquise, les applications restent utilisables sans abonnement récurrent. « Comme avant » finalement.
C'est notamment le cas d'Office 2024 Standard pour Mac qui regroupe les principaux outils de la suite :
- L’indispensable Word pour rédiger et mettre en forme ses documents.
- Excel pour créer des tableaux et gérer ses données.
- PowerPoint pour réaliser des présentations.
- Outlook pour gérer ses e-mails et son calendrier.
- OneNote pour prendre et organiser ses notes
Cette édition fonctionne sur les Mac équipés de processeurs Apple Silicon comme sur les modèles Intel. Elle constitue une solution intéressante pour les particuliers, les étudiants, les indépendants et les petites entreprises qui souhaitent disposer des applications Office sans abonnement.
Attention toutefois : les versions Mac ne proposent pas exactement les mêmes logiciels que leurs équivalents Windows. Access et Publisher, par exemple, ne sont pas disponibles sur macOS.
Quelle version d'Office choisir selon son macOS ?
C'est LE point le plus important avant d'acheter Office pour Mac. La version du système installé sur votre ordinateur Apple détermine en grande partie le choix de la licence.
Pour les Mac fonctionnant sous macOS 15, le choix à privilégier est Office 2024 Standard pour Mac. Cette édition est notamment compatible avec les environnements Apple Silicon et Intel, et bénéficie d'un cycle de support allant jusqu'au 9 octobre 2029, avec des correctifs de sécurité publiés par Microsoft pendant cette période.
Vous utilisez macOS 26 ou macOS 27 ? Office 2024 est également la version à privilégier. Elle permet de profiter d'une suite bureautique récente, sans avoir à s'engager dans un quelconque abonnement Microsoft 365.
La situation est différente pour les Mac qui fonctionnent encore sous macOS 12 Monterey, macOS 13 Ventura ou macOS 14 Sonoma et qui ne peuvent pas évoluer vers Sequoia. Dans ce cas, Office 2021 Standard pour Mac constitue la solution de repli à envisager.
Dès lors, il faut néanmoins avoir conscience d'un point important. Microsoft a mis fin au support d'Office 2021 le 13 octobre 2026. Les applications continuent de fonctionner, mais elles ne reçoivent désormais plus de correctifs de sécurité.
Si votre Mac est compatible avec macOS 15 Sequoia, il est préférable d’effectuer la mise à jour Apple avant de choisir Office 2024. Si ce n'est pas possible, Office 2021 reste une option, avec toutefois cette limite à prendre en compte.
Enfin, si votre ordinateur fonctionne sous macOS 11 Big Sur ou une version antérieure, aucune de ces deux éditions n'est adaptée. Inutile donc de vous orienter vers un achat qui ne correspondrait pas à votre configuration.
Pour connaître la version de macOS installée sur votre Mac, suivez simplement ces étapes :
- Cliquez sur le menu Pomme, en haut à gauche de l'écran.
- Sélectionnez « A propos de ce Mac ».
- La version de macOS apparaît aussitôt dans la fenêtre qui s'ouvre.
Acheter sa licence Office pour Mac chez SOS ORDINATEUR STORE
Une fois la compatibilité vérifiée, reste désormais à choisir où acheter sa licence. SOS ORDINATEUR STORE est une boutique en ligne française spécialisée dans la vente de licences logicielles en téléchargement, notamment pour Windows, Microsoft Office et les antivirus.
En achetant Office 2024 pour Mac chez SOS ORDINATEUR STORE (ou Office 2021 pour les configurations qui nécessitent cette version), on peut profiter de licences qui couvrent un, trois ou cinq Mac, selon la formule choisie.
Vous êtes novices en informatique ? Pas de panique, le fonctionnement est pensé pour rester accessible, y compris donc pour les utilisateurs qui ne sont pas particulièrement à l'aise avec l'installation de logiciels. Après la commande, la licence est envoyée directement par e-mail, accompagnée d'une notice d'installation en français.
Sur Mac, l'activation passe par un fichier spécifique, appelé « serializer », et transmis avec la commande. Il suffit de l'exécuter pour activer les applications. Aucune clé à saisir ni aucun compte Microsoft à rattacher à la licence ne sont nécessaires.
Autre point appréciable, SOS ORDINATEUR STORE propose un accompagnement en français par téléphone six jours sur sept et par e-mail sept jours sur sept. De plus, la boutique annonce une activation garantie pendant les 30 jours suivant l'achat. Si le fichier d'activation rencontre un problème, il est remplacé ou, si cela s'avère impossible, la commande est remboursée. Au-delà de cette période, la boutique s'engage également à remplacer sans délai une licence qui viendrait à être désactivée.
De quoi aborder l'installation avec davantage de sérénité, à condition d'avoir pris le temps de vérifier un élément essentiel avant de passer commande : la version de macOS installée sur son Mac.
