articles.title: DuckLake 1.1 solves the absurd complexity of data lakes at AI scale
articles.text:
DuckLake 1.1 solves the absurd complexity of data lakes at AI scale
How much simpler could a data lakehouse get if an ordinary SQL database kept track of its files? That’s the question in this episode of The New Stack podcast.
DuckLake is an open-source table lakehouse format created by Amsterdam-based DuckLabs that acts as a traffic cop for data management by storing table metadata inside a standard SQL database, rather than scattering manifest files across object storage. Unlike traditional table formats, DuckLake treats lakehouse metadata as a relational database problem. These advanced data lake features, served by Parquet files and SQL databases, reduce the traditional lakehouse complexity.
In October, DuckLake 1.1 launched alongside DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS. The New Stack sat down with Pedro Holanda, lead DuckLake developer and principal engineer at DuckLabs at their Amsterdam headquarters, to talk about the launch. Holanda has contributed to the DuckDB open-source project since it was an early research prototype, and shares the full evolution of DuckLake to our conversation.
“These lakehouse formats exist so people can exchange their database systems without having to do migrations,” Holanda tells The New Stack. Because of the complexity, “you need a database system to keep track of which table has its last version.”
DuckLake applies decades of research, Holanda says, in order to reduce files and therefore complexity at a time of rapid data growth, taking advantage of how everyone who uses database systems is familiar with SQL and how schemas work.
“The simplicity is the way you fetch your data,” Holanda says of DuckLake. “You’re going to issue queries somewhere. The server is going to answer these questions back, and you know exactly which Parquet files you have to read. So the Parquet files don’t change. Just the catalog.”
Maintainers of your data lake often have many maintenance tasks to perform. If you end up with many files, he says, DuckLake lets you glue them into one file to reduce the number of requests. This can also be done across multiple snapshots, further reducing the number of files. It also solves the “small files problem” in streaming data lakes and lakehouses by using inlining and flushing.
Whereas for traditional data lakes, across multiple data sources being inserted at a time, “you end up with so many files, so when you have to query it, you’re going to have to traverse a bunch of metadata files just to figure out which Parquet files you need to read, and then you’re going to have a bunch of Parquet files to read as well,” Holanda says, slowing everything down and frustrating the developer.
DuckLake is known to be fast, simple to use, and not requiring massive server clusters to run. Part of that comes from Parquet being very similar to DuckDB storage: both are columnar and organized in row groups, which keeps the massaging step to a minimum.
“One thing that we realized when we were building DuckLake is that, ‘Hey, we have a database system now, we have a catalog; what if we do this radical idea of storing data on tables?'” he says. “With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.”
“With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.”
During Amazon’s Q3 earnings call in late October, CEO Andy Jassy called out the complexity of moving data between data stores and analytics engines, especially as AWS customers’ data generation continues to increase. Amazon is famous for dogfooding, and Jassy pointed to DuckDB’s solution to this complexity as a reason for its DuckLabs acquisition.
“With our acquisition of DuckLabs, DuckDB will become the universal SQL dialect of AWS storage and analytics, simplifying data processing with a modern analytics engine that is fast, simple to use and ubiquitous, and where customers will be able to write SQL queries once and then execute using any AWS analytics service,” Jassy said. “For the first time in analytics, customers will have zero migration or portability costs between query engines. This is a big deal, and you can imagine how it will also help agents do efficient querying as well.”
DuckDB and DuckLake remain free and open source under the MIT license, overseen by the independent DuckDB Foundation.
Overall, this recent DuckLake release pairs new features with more than 200 bug fixes for quality and stability, and it runs natively in DuckDB.

articles.title: The Hackintosh might be back, with macOS booting on Snapdragon and x86 PCs
articles.text:
In brief: For decades, users who wanted to use macOS without buying a Mac could build a Hackintosh. Hackintoshing became more difficult after Apple transitioned to in-house Arm processors, but at least two projects have recently emerged that aim to revive the practice on Snapdragon and x86 processors.
Users can now try an early version of a new Arm-to-x86 translation layer that aims to support macOS on most recent Intel and AMD processors. Elsewhere, another project has booted the operating system on a Snapdragon-powered Asus Zenbook with basic functionality.
Although Hackintoshes have existed since the 1980s, running macOS on non-Apple devices gained popularity in the early 2000s. Apple's shift from PowerPC to Intel processors in 2006 made the process much easier, since the Intel chips used for Windows devices were more widely available. However, the company's transition to Apple Silicon, a homegrown Arm architecture, was thought to have ended Hackintoshes for good.
 – Miguel C (e/acc) 👁️ (@Acelogic_) October 22, 2026
Snapintosh, which engineer Miguel Cruz revealed last month, might be the first serious effort to break macOS free of Apple Silicon via a Qualcomm Snapdragon SoC. Brief social media clips show him booting the operating system, shifting between various desktop modes, and opening numerous programs on an Asus Zenbook A16 laptop, but much work remains.
Currently, Snapintosh only supports the Zenbook A16's Snapdragon X2 Elite processor, requires a Mac host, and doesn't work on battery power. Furthermore, Wi-Fi, audio, cameras, Bluetooth, sleep, and external displays don't work yet, and the OS can't maintain a stable 60 fps. It remains unclear when a beta will be available on the project's GitHub repository.
 – Miguel C (e/acc) 👁️ (@Acelogic_) October 20, 2026
Meanwhile, engineer Tyler Smith is developing Stela, which uses an Arm-to-x86 translator to run macOS on a much broader range of PCs. The open beta supports Intel Nehalem or later and AMD Bulldozer or later. It also only requires 8GB of RAM and an Nvidia GTX 16-series or newer graphics card.
To try Stela, download the beta from the GitHub repository, run the setup executable on a Windows device, and select a USB stick as the installation destination. The online installer requires 8GB of free storage space, while the offline version requires 32GB, and the target device's installation drive requires 60GB. Like Snapintosh, Stela doesn't yet support Wi-Fi or audio, but Bluetooth works.
Interested users can discuss Stela and share tips on the project's Discord server.

articles.title: Here are our favorite deals from REI’s giant Holiday Sale
articles.text:
Black Friday has become a shopping season of its own, with retailers once again offering discounts well ahead of the actual shopping holiday. We’ve already rounded up some of the best early Black Friday deals we’ve come across, but if you’re looking to save on outdoor gear or pick up something for an upcoming trip, REI’s annual Holiday Sale, which runs through November 23rd, is worth checking out.
Here are our favorite deals from REI’s giant Holiday Sale
From Garmin watches to seasonal camping gear, REI is offering a slate of deep discounts ahead of Black Friday.
As usual, the outdoor retailer is offering discounts on everything from smartwatches to camping equipment. In some cases, we’re seeing some of the lowest prices we’ve seen on our favorite wearables, including Garmin’s Forerunner 570, while gadgets like the InReach Mini 3 are also receiving sizable discounts. REI members can also use promo code HOLIDAY2026 to save 20 percent on one full-price item, plus an additional 20 percent on one REI Outlet item.
To save you time, we’ve sifted through the deluge of discounts to find an assortment of deals we recommend here at The Verge. We’ve also noted when competing retailers are offering lower prices on the same items, so you can be sure you’re getting the best deal possible.
Smartwatches and fitness tech
Garmin Forerunner 570
Garmin’s Forerunner 570 features a bright OLED display, skin temperature sensors, and a built-in speaker and microphone for taking calls. It also offers multiband GPS, personalized training plans, and up to 11 days of battery life.
Garmin Venu 4
Garmin’s Venu 4 is geared toward the average athlete, offering heart rate alerts, detailed sleep insights, guided meditation, and a wheelchair mode. It also introduces caffeine and alcohol tracking, along with Garmin Coach, which tailors workouts to your fitness history, sleep, and recovery.
- REI, Amazon, and Best Buy are also selling the Garmin Lily 2 Active for $249.99 ($50 off), which is its lowest price to date. The stylish smartwatch is a great budget-friendly Garmin, especially for people with smaller wrists. Like the standard Lily 2, it offers basic fitness tracking, notifications, and up to five days of battery life; however, the so-called “Active” model adds a physical button, built-in GPS, and support for more sports tracking. Read our Lily 2 review.
- The Garmin Vivoactive 6 has returned to its all-time low of $249.99 ($50 off) at Amazon, Walmart, and REI. The fitness watch offers up to 11 days of battery life and tracks a range of workouts, including walking, running, cycling, HIIT, golf, and more. It also provides extensive health monitoring, including wrist-based heart rate detection, menstrual cycle and pregnancy tracking, and a customizable morning report that summarizes helpful health-related info. However, it lacks ECG compatibility, though it does have a slightly slimmer profile than its predecessor.
Garmin Fenix 8
The Garmin Fenix 8 is a premium multisport watch that features a speaker, mic, and on-device assistant for calls, timers, and voice commands. It also offers elite battery life, dual-frequency GPS, and robust sensors. Read our review.
- The Wahoo Kickr V6 Smart Trainer is on sale at REI for $679.99 ($170 off). Like the more affordable Kickr Core 2 we covered in July, the Kickr V6 turns your existing bike into an indoor exercise bike, with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity for pairing with apps like Zwift. However, the higher-end trainer offers up to 2,200W of resistance and can replicate inclines of up to 20 percent, compared to the Core 2’s 1,800W and 16 percent. It also provides more accurate power measurements and is designed so that indoor rides feel more natural.
Phone accessories and entertainment
EcoFlow Rapid Magnetic Power Bank
EcoFlow’s Rapid Magnetic Power Bank is a 10,000mAh Qi2 battery that can snap to the back of your device if you’re using a newer iPhone or select Android devices, thus supplying it with up to 15W of power. It also includes a built-in USB-C cable that can provide up to 65W of power to larger devices, including a 13-inch MacBook Air.
- If you own an older iPhone with a Lightning port, you can grab InfinityLab’s InstantGo 10,000 Power Bank for $41.93 (about $28 off) at REI. The portable battery features a 10,000mAh capacity and a built-in Lightning cable, making it a solid all-in-one option for days when you won’t be near an outlet. It also supports passthrough charging, so you can charge your phone and the power bank at the same time.
- DJI’s Osmo Mobile 8 is on sale for around $128.99 ($21 off) at REI, Amazon, and Best Buy, which is $10 shy of its best price to date. The smartphone gimbal supports 360-degree horizontal rotation and Apple’s DockKit, which allows the gimbal to track and follow pets and people across a wider range of camera apps. This discounted Advanced Tracking Combo also includes a multifunctional module for tracking people and pets, as well as a built-in tripod and extension rod that make it easier to film yourself without someone behind the camera.
Soundcore Liberty 5
The Soundcore Liberty 5 feature adaptive noise cancellation and support for Dolby Audio, along with six swappable tips so you can find the right fit. They also sport an IP55 rating for water and dust resistance and can last up to 48 hours with the included charging case.
- You can buy Soundcore’s AeroFit 2 for $79.99 ($20 off) at REI, Amazon, and Best Buy, which is $2 shy of their lowest price to date. Their open-ear design lets you listen to music while staying vigilant in your surroundings; they also feature adjustable ear hooks for a secure fit, IP55 water and dust resistance, and up to 42 hours of battery life with the included charging case.
Anker Nebula P1 projector
Anker’s Nebula P1 is a portable 1080p projector with built-in Google TV and two detachable Bluetooth speakers that deliver better sound than many all-in-one portable projectors. It offers 650 ANSI lumens of brightness and can project images up to 180 inches, while the speakers last up to 20 hours on a charge.
Communication and safety gear
Garmin InReach Mini 3 Plus
The Mini 3 Plus is identical to the standard model in that it allows you to stay connected while off the grid; however, it also features an audible siren and the ability to send photos and voice messages, in addition to standard texts.
- Garmin’s base InReach Mini 3 is available from REI, Amazon, and Garmin for around $349 ($100 off), nearly matching its lowest price to date. Like the Mini 2, the rugged, palm-sized satellite communicator lets you send texts, share your location, check the weather, and trigger SOS alerts when you’re off the grid, all while offering battery life that can outlast your average smartphone. Unlike the prior version, though, it features a color touchscreen, which makes it easier to navigate menus and bang out messages.
- Garmin’s InReach Messenger Plus is also on sale at REI, Amazon, and direct from Garmin for $299.99 ($100 off), matching its best price to date. The subscription-based Plus model provides satellite connectivity and access to emergency services like the aforementioned InReach Mini 3, except it can also send photos and audio clips in addition to standard text messages.
- The Chapter MIPS Bike Helmet is on sale starting at around $112.39 ($41 off) at REI, which nearly matches its best price to date. The lightweight helmet features a hidden PopLock for securing it with a U-lock or chain. It also has a sleek visor and a Micro-USB taillight with 30 lumens of brightness, one that automatically turns on when magnetically attached to the helmet.
- Garmin’s Varia RTL515 Radar Taillight is on sale at REI and Amazon for $149.99 ($50 off), which is about $10 less than its all-time low. The headlight combines a bright LED light with a rearview radar that, when paired with a compatible device, warns you of cars approaching from behind from up to 153 yards away.
BCA Tracker 3 Plus Avalanche Transceiver
The Tracker 3 Plus is a pocketable, lightweight avalanche beacon designed to help locate people buried in snow. It features a real-time display, lights to guide searchers, and tools for finding multiple people. It also comes with a harness and batteries.
Camping and travel gear
Exped MegaMat Duo
The MegaMat Duo is a four-inch, self-inflating mattress that’s become one of our favorites thanks to its extra-wide design. It uses a combination of open-cell polyurethane foam and generous padding for comfort, which helps keep you warm when temperatures dip. It also makes for a stellar air mattress for guests.
- A small chair is nice to have for lounging by the campfire, and REI’s Flexlite Camp Chair is a great option now that it’s down to around $67.39 (about $22 off) in multiple colors at REI. It features an aluminum frame, a stable four-leg design, and a ripstop polyester seat with water and stain resistance. When you’re done, it also folds down quickly into a drawstring bag, so you can throw it in your car.
Kelty Low Loveseat
The Kelty Low Loveseat is a sturdy, low-profile camp chair built for two. It features a steel frame, a padded seat, and extra-large cup holders for your drinks or gear. It also includes a padded roll-tote storage bag, making it easy to transport when it’s folded down.
- REI is currently selling its Magma 30 Sleeping Bag in a variety of sizes starting at $243.93 ($105 off). The bag uses 850-fill-power, water-resistant down for warmth and weighs under 20 ounces, depending on the size, making it a great budget pick if you’re looking to get into ultralight backpacking. It also includes a hood to help retain heat, extra room around the feet, and a terrific zipper design that’s less likely to snag when you’re crawling in or out.
REI Siesta Hooded 20 Sleeping Bag
The Siesta prioritizes comfort with a roomy rectangular shape that gives you space to stretch out. The synthetic sleeping bag features an insulated hood — one that’s spacious enough to accommodate a real pillow — along with multiple zipper configurations so you can vent your feet or fully unzip it into a quilt-like blanket.
Rumpl Original Puffy Blanket
Rumpl’s classic lightweight blanket features synthetic insulation for warmth, a weather-resistant outer shell, and a stuff sack. It also comes in an array of attractive designs and pairs with Rumpl’s Cape Clip, so you can wear it hands-free.
- Osprey’s Atmos AG 65 Pack is on sale in several colors and size configurations for around $258.93 ($112 off) at REI, which is one of the lowest prices we’ve seen. The 65-liter pack — which remains a go-to option for The Verge’s own Brandon Widder — is loaded with all sorts of bells and whistles, including an integrated rain cover, a floating top lid, and plenty of compression straps. The hallmark, though, is the ventilation system, which leverages a 3D-suspended mesh for comfort and breathability, making it a great pick for multi-day trips.
- REI’s Ruckpack Waist Pack is on sale for $33.69 ($12 off) at REI, which is one of the best prices we’ve seen as of late. Made from a water-repellent material, this small adjustable bag can be worn around your waist or across your body and features three interior pockets for keeping your essentials organized.
Sea to Summit Hanging Toiletry Bag
Sea to Summit’s small toiletry bag lets you keep all of your essentials close at hand for weekend getaways. It features a water–resistant fabric and a convenient hanging hook, along with internal mesh pockets so you can quickly find whatever it is you need.
- The JetBoil Stash Cooking System is a compact, lightweight cooking system that’s currently down to $123.69 (about $41 off) at REI, which is one of the lowest prices we’ve seen all year. It features a standalone stove with a titanium burner and a 0.8-liter cooking pot, allowing you to boil water or heat food at your campsite. The pot comes with a lid and a pour handle, too, and everything can be stowed inside the pot when you’re finished, making it exceptionally easy to pack up.
Sea to Summit Aeros Premium Pillow
Sea to Summit’s lightweight, inflatable camping pillow features a soft memory foam layer, adjustable firmness, and a curved design that cradles your head. It’s also quick to inflate and includes patches to keep it from sliding while you sleep.
- You can buy the ultralight Nemo Tensor in multiple sizes starting at REI for $131.93 (about $88 off). Designed for backpacking, the four-season sleeping pad offers 3.5 inches of cushioning and insulation to keep you warm in colder conditions, with a 5.4 R-value. The nylon construction is also relatively quiet, which, frankly, isn’t the case with many of the camping pads we’ve used over the years.
- Nemo’s Stargaze Evo-X is on sale for $99.99 ($80 off) at REI, which is a great price for the surprisingly portable camping chair. The plush, versatile chair automatically reclines when you lean back, making it ideal for relaxing around the campsite (and stargazing). It also features a padded headrest, two cupholders, and a folding frame. And did we mention it swings? Because it swings.
- REI’s Wonderland Cot is down to $187.39 ($62 off) at REI. The foldable cot — which is designed more for car camping than anything else — features a spacious, padded sleeping surface, an adjustable backrest, and a sturdy aluminum and steel frame that supports up to 300 pounds. The new version also comes with a webbing carrying strap, making it easier to lug around than prior models.
Headlamps and lighting
Mpowerd Luci Solar String Lights: Color
Mpowerd’s solar-powered string lights are perfect for camping or a backyard shindig. The 18-foot string can display six colors and last up to 15 hours on a single charge; the case also doubles as a charger, allowing you to top off your phone in a pinch.
- Black Diamond’s Spot, the newer version of the Spot 400 headlamp, is on sale for $47.89 ($12 off) at REI. It offers up to 450 lumens of adjustable brightness, up from 400, along with red night vision and an IPX7 water-resistance rating. You can also choose to power it with standard AAA batteries or Black Diamond’s rechargeable battery.
- The Petzl Tikka is on sale at REI for $18.77 (about $16 off). The basic headlamp is a great option that features a max output of 350 lumens, tilt functionality, and an IPX4 rating, making it safe to use in light rain. It also features a lock function that prevents it from accidentally turning on when packed.
Black Diamond Moji Plus Lantern
The Moji Plus offers 200 lumens of warm, dimmable light and adjustable brightness, along with an IPX4 rating for water resistance. It also features a double-hook design and the same dual-fuel tech as the Spot 400 Headlamp, meaning you can use it with standard AAAs or Black Diamond’s rechargeable BD 1500 Li-ion battery.
- The Nite Ize Radiant 314 — which is currently down to $23.77 (about $22 off) at REI — provides 314 lumens of brightness, an impact-resistant design, and an IPX4 rating for water resistance. The rechargeable lantern can also last up to 96 hours on a single charge, while the built-in power bank can provide an extra boost of power to your phone in a pinch.
- Luminaid’s Max 2-in-1 Power Lantern, which now inflates with a simple twist, is available for $47.19 (about $13 off) at REI. The nifty lantern delivers up to 200 lumens of light and lasts up to 50 hours; it also doubles as a portable phone charger, recharges either via solar power or USB, and folds flat.

articles.title: Commemorative plaque at Denny’s booth where Nvidia was born has been removed — sign removed in wake of Jensen's scandals, marked 'the booth that launched a $1 trillion company'
articles.text:
Commemorative plaque at Denny’s booth where Nvidia was born has been removed — sign removed in wake of Jensen's scandals, marked 'the booth that launched a $1 trillion company'
Jensen Huang once worked at Denny's as a seasonal dishwasher, busboy, and waiter.
Jensen Huang was one of the American success stories in Silicon Valley, where he had his humble beginnings as a seasonal dishwasher, busboy, and waiter at his nearby Denny’s before he rose to stardom as the head of Nvidia. The diner honored this achievement with a plaque at the booth where Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem met after their working hours and first planned the inception of Nvidia. However, NBC News said that the sign has since been removed following Huang’s spectacular fall from grace and resignation from the company.
Unfortunately, employees say that the commemorative plaque, which read, “The booth that launched a $1 trillion company,” has been removed. It remains unclear who ordered the removal, though, so we reached out to Denny’s for comment and will update the story if they answer.
Despite being a billionaire, the former Nvidia CEO is known for keeping in touch with his roots. He has been spotted several times eating street food and enjoying local fast food in the various cities that he visits. He even once dragged the 35 Taiwanese industry chiefs to a restaurant in Taipei, earning that event the moniker “trillion-dollar banquet.” This “man of the people” persona has made him quite a popular figure among some people, fueling the Jensanity hype, especially in his home country of Taiwan.
We also saw this side of Jensen during the unveiling of the plaque in 2023, after Nvidia hit a $1 trillion valuation, when he balanced 10 plates and served food during the event. The restaurant also put up a food truck and served “Nvidia Breakfast Bytes” at GTC 2025, which consisted of four sausage links served with four buttermilk silver dollar pancakes and some syrup, and was available for a limited time for under $5 in all Denny’s branches across the country.
This move is just another sign of Jensen’s sudden downfall. He was still the leader of one of the most valuable companies in the world a couple of weeks ago, evangelizing artificial intelligence to anyone willing to listen. Today finds a totally different reality, with sources saying that he looked “broken and shattered,” and he even called himself “a piece of sh--” as he left the company he built for over 30 years after the board ousted him.
There is no telling yet what’s next for Jensen Huang. Elon Musk has reportedly offered him a position, saying that it “would be an honor” to hire the person who was arguably one of the biggest driving forces in today’s AI industry, but he’s also facing numerous investigations from both his company, Congress, and the FBI. More importantly, Jensen will have to deal with the fallout of the revelations on his public image and personal life.
Download the Tom's Hardware app for up-to-the-minute updates on iOS and Android. Also follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.

Jowi Morales is a tech enthusiast with years of experience working in the industry. He’s been writing with several tech publications since 2021, where he’s been interested in tech hardware and consumer electronics.

articles.title: Una verdadera pesadilla: este malware podría seguir accediendo a tu Gmail aunque cambies de contraseña
articles.text:
No es novedad que el software malicioso está evolucionando a un ritmo altísimo y que la inteligencia artificial generativa está simplificando la creación y distribución de amenazas cada vez más complejas. Por ello no resulta una absoluta sorpresa que añada capacidades que desafían cualquier avance que se logre en materia de ciberseguridad. El caso del malware Remus es uno de los que más ha llamado la atención en los últimos días, pues al parecer es un infostealer que puede seguir accediendo a tu Gmail aunque cambies de contraseña.
Según reporta Neowin, los investigadores de Hudson Rock pusieron a prueba la más reciente versión del malware Remus, cuyos desarrolladores afirman que incluye un nivel de persistencia que lo convierte en una pesadilla para los usuarios de Gmail.
Los creadores de Remus sostienen que el malware permite acceder a un Gmail comprometido directamente desde su aplicación de escritorio, mediante una interfaz similar a la de un cliente de correo electrónico convencional. Al parecer, este puede continuar dando acceso al contenido de una cuenta comprometida a pesar de que las víctimas actualicen su contraseña o cierren todas las sesiones que mantienen activas.
Si lo que dicen los creadores del malware Remus es cierto, estamos hablando de un exploit de gran complejidad y severidad. Los expertos que han estudiado el infostealer de Gmail indican, no obstante, que algunas de las afirmaciones más resonantes se deberían tomar con pinzas. Sobre todo, porque no hay datos técnicos precisos que soporten lo que los piratas informáticos promocionan.
La nueva versión del malware Remus podría entrar a tu Gmail aunque cambies la contraseña
Los expertos de Hudson Rock les preguntaron a los creadores del malware Remus cómo funcionaba su acceso persistente a Gmail. Estos se negaron a brindar detalles puntuales que pudieran llevar a una solución de la brecha que permite el ataque. Aun así, indicaron que su infostealer es lo suficientemente inteligente como para evadir las tecnologías antifraude de Google.
También comentaron que lo que hace el malware Remus es interactuar de forma breve con la memoria del navegador web para acceder a la información almacenada allí. Los desarrolladores del software malicioso dicen no recolectar ni clonar las cookies del navegador para interceptar los códigos de verificación.
Los especialistas en ciberseguridad que han analizado el comportamiento del malware Remus y su presunto acceso persistente a Gmail no creen que, como estos promocionan, se esté explotando una vulnerabilidad de día cero en la plataforma de correo electrónico. Según explican, la evidencia existente no es la suficientemente amplia o detallada como para convalidar esa afirmación.
En tal sentido, la explicación más lógica del funcionamiento del malware es que Remus puede establecer una autorización reutilizable que sirve mientras mantiene el acceso a un navegador con una sesión iniciada. No obstante, la aserción del nivel de persistencia sobre las cuentas de Gmail infectadas podría estar exagerada. Sea como sea, cambiar las contraseñas, activar la verificación en dos pasos y usar llaves de acceso (passkeys) siguen siendo recomendaciones a considerar si crees que tu cuenta de correo electrónico puede estar en peligro.

articles.title: Open-source 3D printer uses $30 of classic LEGO bricks for 92% of its build — $180 "Studprint" relies on just 13 non-LEGO parts and prints a Benchy in 1.25 hours
articles.text:
Open-source 3D printer uses $30 of classic LEGO bricks for 92% of its build — $180 "Studprint" relies on just 13 non-LEGO parts and prints a Benchy in 1.25 hours
A traditional bed slinger made mostly of LEGO; the printbed, leadscrews, and even the gantry are LEGO.
Adam Turaj, a Mechatronics Engineering student at the University of Waterloo, built an open-source LEGO 3D printer named “Studprint” with only 13 pieces of the printer not made out of LEGO. The bill of materials only totals $173.35, with $30 of the budget going to LEGO pieces that comprise 92% of the whole build. Turaj’s project got him flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, where he got to meet Prusa CMO Zack Freedman and presented Studprint to over 4,000 people at the event.
Earlier this year, Hack Club posted a challenge called Infill, calling makers and hobbyists to design their own 3D printers from scratch and receive a $350 grant to build their printers. Whoever submits a benchy with their printer gets a chance to be flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, and Turaj was one of them.
Turaj joined this challenge, designing his LEGO 3D printer in SOLIDWORKS. He named the project Studprint, referring to the studs on a LEGO brick. What takes this project even farther is that Turaj decided he would only use “classical LEGO,” avoiding LEGO Technic pieces wherever possible. Looking at the repository’s images of the CAD designs, you would easily mistake it for a virtual LEGO builder.
Turaj shared an image of the bill of materials (BOM) on the GitHub repository for his build, showing a final build price of $173.35. There are three major electronics components in the printer: the first is the BTT SKR Pico V1.0, a control board commonly used in open-source 3D printers like the Voron V0; for wireless capability, a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is used; and the whole printer is powered by a Mean Well LRS-150-24 switching power supply — with all three components priced at around $25 each. This printer is built with the backbone of a true DIY 3D-printer build, unlike this cute LEGO 3D printer we covered last year that used a 3D printing pen.
There are five NEMA 17 stepper motors, also popular in 3D printers, whether open- or closed-source. Four of the motors control the axes, while the fifth is used to feed filament to the Trianglelab V6 Extruder. The rest of the 3D printer is made of $30 worth of LEGO pieces; even the build plate is a block of LEGO. Turaj’s only print shown on the GitHub repository is a Benchy, sliced in Klipper and printed in 1.25 hours; it’s surprisingly good considering the leadscrews are all LEGO pieces.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Jhet Borja is a serial hobbyist who was taking apart toys from childhood and sketching inventions. He now loves doing DIY projects ranging from designing custom 3D-printed parts, building PCs and keyboards, all the way to woodworking. If he's not getting his hands dirty, he's probably brainstorming his next project.

articles.title: Pour écouler les surplus de Nvidia, Jensen Huang aurait financé des start-up IA
articles.text:
Jensen Huang a quitté la présidence, la direction générale et le conseil d’administration de Nvidia le 12 novembre, avec effet immédiat, rattrapé par l’affaire Alice Huang et l’enquête interne qu’elle a déclenchée. Colette Kress, directrice financière depuis 2013, assure l’intérim pendant que le conseil cherche un successeur permanent. Leurs derniers mois de cohabitation racontent un désaccord profond sur les milliards engagés par Nvidia pour soutenir ses propres clients.
La réunion d’août où Huang a humilié celle qui le remplace
Au cours d’une réunion organisée en août avec les cadres financiers du groupe, Jensen Huang aurait interrompu la présentation de Colette Kress pour la qualifier de « lapin pris dans les phares ». Il l’aurait aussi décrite en directrice financière « de reporting », incapable à ses yeux de contribuer à la stratégie ou de peser sur les grandes décisions. L’anecdote est sortie cette semaine, dans la foulée de la promotion de l’intéressée.
Lire aussi : Mémoire vive : l’espoir d’une baisse des prix avant 2030 vient de mourir
Le différend portait sur les garanties financières accordées aux acheteurs de puces Nvidia, fournisseurs de cloud émergents et promoteurs de centres de données en tête. Nico Caprez, vice-président du groupe et gendre de Jensen Huang, pilotait une partie de ces montages. Colette Kress aurait cherché à le recadrer, en demandant comment évaluer ces garanties, en calculer le rendement, et si les clients ainsi soutenus pourraient seulement honorer leurs commandes.
Le dossier le plus lourd liait OpenAI à un centre de données de l’Ohio, appelé à héberger pour environ 300 milliards de dollars de puces Nvidia. Les premières discussions évoquaient une garantie couvrant 8 gigawatts de capacité, valorisée jusqu’à 250 milliards de dollars. La directrice financière aurait obtenu de réduire l’enveloppe de moitié avant la signature, le 17 août, d’un accord dont la première tranche couvre 4,25 gigawatts. La fuite du montant initial avait déjà coûté cet été 5 % à l’action, soit près de 250 milliards de dollars de capitalisation.
Une « avalanche » à 279 milliards de dollars, et des clients financés pour suivre
Jensen Huang s’alarmait lui-même en privé d’une « avalanche » d’engagements d’achat de galettes de silicium et de mémoire, pendant que les grands fournisseurs de cloud regardaient vers des puces concurrentes. Les engagements d’approvisionnement du groupe, publiés fin août, sont passés de 119 à 279 milliards de dollars en un seul trimestre, principalement pour réserver de la mémoire.
Ces montages alimentent depuis des mois le soupçon d’un financement circulaire : Nvidia investit dans des sociétés d’IA, qui utilisent ces fonds pour lui acheter des processeurs, et la demande paraît d’autant plus solide. La promesse initiale de septembre 2025, jusqu’à 100 milliards de dollars pour équiper OpenAI, a fondu en chemin, et Huang répétait que ce montant n’avait « jamais été un engagement ». Le groupe a finalement investi 30 milliards de dollars dans OpenAI et 10 milliards dans Anthropic, en plus des garanties de location. Sur X, Huang balayait la critique : « S’agit-il d’un financement circulaire ? Non. » Ces soutiens auraient pourtant aussi servi à absorber les volumes commandés en trop auprès de TSMC, à rebours du discours officiel sur une demande dépassant de loin l’offre.
Plusieurs accords de financement sont depuis suspendus, et les prochains passeront sous l’œil de la direction et du conseil d’administration. La facture atterrit déjà chez les consommateurs : le virage de Nvidia vers la mémoire LPDDR, celle des smartphones, a asséché le marché. Counterpoint anticipait dès novembre 2025 un doublement du prix de la mémoire serveur avant fin 2026, et PC, consoles comme smartphones encaissent ces hausses depuis des mois.

Source : The Wall Street Journal

articles.title: Las mejores ofertas previas al Black Friday: desde móviles de gama alta hasta televisores y auriculares
articles.text:
Quedan poco menos de dos semanas para la llegada del Black Friday, pero las tiendas están dando un buen adelanto de ofertas en tecnología. Por ello, en este artículo vamos a repasar los mejores chollos que están ahora mismo disponibles en móviles, auriculares y más.
- Google Pixel 11 Pro por 788 euros, un precio mucho más ajustado en uno de los mejores móviles de la marca.
- AirPods Pro 3 por 199 euros, un buen precio si somos del Club Carrefour.
- Samsung Galaxy S26+ por 896,22 euros, un móvil grande y con una buena pantalla.
- Sony WH-1000XM4C por 199 euros, unos auriculares cómodos y con muy buena cancelación de ruido.
- LG OLED B6 por 1.099 euros, un televisor de 65 pulgadas con tratamiento antirreflejos.
Google Pixel 11 Pro
El Google Pixel 11 Pro ha recibido una de las mejores ofertas que hemos visto durante las semanas previas al Black Friday. MediaMarkt lo tiene por 788 euros utilizando el cupón PIXEL111PARATI. Además, este cupón también sirve con el resto de móviles de la gama:
- El Google Pixel 11 se queda por un precio de 688 euros.
- El Google 11 Pro XL se queda por un precio de 1.088 euros.
Google Pixel 11 Pro (256 GB)
AirPods Pro 3
Si eres miembro del Club Carrefour y accedes a la app Mi Carrefour, puedes aprovechar la oferta que tiene la tienda en los AirPods Pro 3, ya que su precio baja hasta los 199 euros. Son unos auriculares especialmente cómodos que tienen bastante autonomía (entre seis y siete horas), la cancelación activa de ruido mejora con respecto a la generación anterior y cuentan con un sensor de frecuencia cardíaca.
Samsung Galaxy S26+
El Samsung Galaxy S26+ también ha bajado (y bastante) de precio; Amazon lo tiene ahora mismo por 896,22 euros. Se trata de un móvil grande con pantalla de 6,7 pulgadas que ofrece una resolución QHD+, su sistema operativo estará actualizado durante muchos años y tiene un buen sistema de cámaras.
Samsung Galaxy S26+ (256 GB)
Sony WH-1000XM4C
Los Sony WH-1000XM4C son los auriculares en la última versión que ha lanzado la marca para implementar la batería extraíble. Por 199 euros en El Corte Inglés, es una opción de compra interesante dada la calidad de sonido que ofrecen, pero también lo son por su cancelación activa de ruido y por lo cómodos que resultan incluso utilizándolos durante horas.
LG OLED B6
MediaMarkt ha lanzado una muy buena oferta en la LG OLED B6, una smart TV que, por 1.099 euros, incluye de regalo la barra de sonido LG S40T. En lo que se refiere al televisor, viene con un panel con tecnología OLED de 65 pulgadas que cuenta con tratamiento antirreflejos. También es compatible con los formatos de imagen HDR10+ y Dolby Vision, así como el formato de audio Dolby Atmos, y su pantalla ofrece una tasa de refresco de 120 Hz.
