articles.title: Cette marque française a capté plus de 20 % des véhicules électriques en leasing social
articles.text:
Le leasing social 2026 est encore disponible. 50 000 véhicules électriques peuvent être commandés par des ménages aux revenus modestes auprès des constructeurs européens, dans le cadre d’un leasing de trois ans à un tarif très avantageux. Parmi les marques ayant profité du leasing social pour distribuer leurs véhicules, on retrouve Citroën, qui a déjà capté plus de 20 % du volume total de véhicules en leasing social pour cette édition 2026.
Plus d’un dossier sur deux au sein du groupe Stellantis
Le constructeur aux chevrons a réussi à optimiser l’utilisation du leasing social. Citroën compte déjà 12 300 véhicules commandés en leasing social, ce qui correspond à plus de 20 % des 50 000 véhicules prévus dans l’enveloppe budgétaire allouée au dispositif gouvernemental.
Mais aussi, cela représente plus d’un dossier sur deux parmi les dossiers de leasing social des marques du groupe Stellantis. Citroën démontre alors sa performance sur le marché des véhicules électriques accessibles. Le constructeur français a bien profité de la plateforme Smart Car pour se constituer une gamme de véhicules électriques abordables.
Deux modèles bien adaptés au leasing social
Pour le leasing social, Citroën profite d’un réseau de distributeurs étoffé qui crée une certaine proximité avec les clients. Mais ce qui aide aussi les chiffres de vente de Citroën dans le cadre du leasing social, ce sont ses deux modèles électriques abordables : la citadine ë-C3 et le SUV ë-C3 Aircross.
La Citroën ë-C3 débute à partir de 94 euros par mois en motorisation Autonomie Urbaine, soit avec le moteur de 113 chevaux et la batterie de 30 kWh pour environ 200 km d’autonomie. Une voiture destinée à la ville et aux petits trajets.
Pour un peu plus de polyvalence, la motorisation Autonomie Confort, avec une batterie de 44 kWh, passe à 99 euros par mois. Elle permet d’atteindre un peu plus de 300 km d’autonomie.
Si la Citroën ë-C3 est trop petite pour vous, vous pouvez opter pour son grand frère, le SUV ë-C3 Aircross, avec toujours le moteur de 113 chevaux et la batterie de 44 kWh pour 309 km d’autonomie en entrée de gamme. Son loyer débute à 109 euros par mois. Si l’autonomie est trop faible, la version Autonomie Étendue utilise le même moteur de 113 chevaux avec une batterie de 54 kWh pour 400 km en cycle WLTP, avec un loyer qui débute à 114 euros par mois.
Des tarifs accessibles pour des voitures électriques simples et qui vont à l’essentiel. Toutefois, la version Citroën ë-C3 Autonomie Urbaine à 94 euros par mois semble être le plus mauvais choix, car son autonomie est vraiment trop réduite pour en faire une voiture polyvalente et elle ne comprend pas la recharge rapide de série. Pour 5 euros de plus par mois, la version Autonomie Confort offre bien plus d’autonomie et la recharge rapide de série.

articles.title: Cursor confirms security breach led to malicious Claude Code extension
articles.text:
Cursor confirmed it suffered a security breach that let hackers distribute a malicious Claude Code extension through its marketplace after stealing credentials from AI infrastructure provider Fireworks AI.
The breach also let attackers access internal systems and steal customer data, including historical AI coding-agent traces containing unredacted credentials that were later used to compromise additional services.
The breach was disclosed in a new incident report published Friday, which explains how attackers distributed malicious versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension through Cursor's marketplace on October 29.
The attack exposed up to 5,000 developers to malware that installed persistent SSH backdoors.
Cursor is an AI-powered code editor built on Microsoft's open-source Visual Studio Code (VS Code), allowing developers to write, modify, and debug software using AI assistants.
According to Cursor, the attack began when hackers obtained an access key stored on Fireworks AI, a third-party provider used for AI model training and inference.
The attackers used the exposed key to copy data from a read-only storage bucket Cursor used to share information with Fireworks.
This bucket contained historical AI coding-agent traces, mostly from 2025, collected from users who had not enabled Privacy Mode and whose data could be used for model training. Some of these traces contained unredacted API credentials, allowing the attackers to access additional Cursor systems.
Cursor says fewer than 0.05% of users had coding-agent traces exposed, while fewer than 0.01% of customers had API credentials compromised.
Using the exposed credentials, the hackers stole data from several of Cursor's software-as-a-service (SaaS) tools, including:
- Archived, non-production Cursor source code repositories, some containing business contact information.
- Limited customer support information and email conversations.
- Product usage metrics and customer contact details.
- Summaries of some AI coding-agent conversations.
- Credentials that customers had previously shared with Cursor's support team.
Cursor says its monitoring systems detected the unauthorized activity, leading the company to revoke the Fireworks access key, rotate exposed credentials, and investigate additional unauthorized access.
As the investigation progressed, Cursor temporarily turned off some internal and product services as a precaution.
However, the attackers had already obtained a credential that allowed them to distribute extensions through Cursor's marketplace.
On October 29, the hackers used that credential to publish malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension on Cursor's VS Code extension marketplace.
"On October 29, using a stolen credential from the exposed data from our internal system, the attacker placed malicious, unauthorized copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace," Cursor explained.
The attack did not compromise Anthropic's legitimate extension or Open VSX, the extension marketplace Cursor uses.
The malicious extensions, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, were available for approximately 11 hours before Cursor removed them.
As BleepingComputer previously reported, the attackers modified the legitimate Claude Code extension to execute malicious JavaScript that attempted to install persistent SSH backdoors on developers' computers.
The malware collected system information, installed an attacker-controlled SSH key, attempted to enable SSH access, and configured persistence mechanisms to maintain remote access.
However, security researchers found coding errors that likely prevented the backdoor from working on many Windows and macOS systems where SSH was not already enabled.
Cursor estimates that up to 5,000 users who requested affected extension versions during the exposure window may have received the malicious builds.
The company says its production infrastructure, official application releases, customer code repositories, and code and prompts belonging to users with Privacy Mode enabled were not affected.
Cursor says it has moved all inference traffic away from Fireworks, revoked and rotated exposed credentials, rebuilt its extension marketplace, and redeployed its production infrastructure as a precaution.
Customers who installed or updated to the affected Claude Code extension during the attack are advised to follow Cursor's remediation guidance.
Black October
The incident comes amid a wave of attacks targeting AI developer platforms that cybersecurity company Wiz has dubbed "Black October".
These attacks targeted development infrastructure to steal authentication credentials, especially those providing access to AI models.
Stolen credentials have been used for unauthorized AI inference, generating substantial charges for affected customers, with some incidents also linked to attempts at AI model distillation.
The attacks have affected numerous companies, including Railway, Northflank, Lightning AI, OpenCode, and Warp.
At Railway, attackers stole customer authentication secrets, which were later used to generate approximately $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges. OpenCode also reported exposed API keys and unauthorized AI usage.
Fireworks AI was also affected, disclosing multiple security breaches in October, including one involving exposed API keys and tokens and another in which attackers accessed development machines through a compromised third-party cloud provider.
The Fireworks incidents also affected other customers, including Notion, which recently disclosed that AI chat transcripts from a small number of workspaces were exposed.

articles.title: Black Friday 2026 : voici la technique la plus rapide pour vérifier si un message provient vraiment d’Amazon
articles.text:
Un colis bloqué en douane, une commande suspecte à annuler, un compte sur le point d’être suspendu…
Chaque année, la période du Black Friday, qui tombe officiellement le 27 novembre en 2026 (mais des promotions sont déjà disponibles avant), est idéale pour les escrocs qui usurpent l’identité d’Amazon, parce que les clients s’attendent justement à recevoir des notifications de la plateforme.
Dans un mail envoyé à ses clients français à la mi-novembre, Amazon conseille une solution simple, qui consiste à lui demander directement si le message est authentique.
Transférer le message suspect
Quand on reçoit un mail, un SMS ou un appel qui prétend venir d’Amazon, il suffit de transférer le mail douteux à l’adresse [email protected], ou d’y décrire le message reçu.
Amazon répond en quelques instants pour confirmer, ou non, qu’il en est l’expéditeur, et recommande de ne pas cliquer, rappeler ou répondre avant d’avoir cette réponse. Chaque demande déclenche aussi un signalement automatique auprès de ses équipes internes, et l’entreprise dit ensuite surveiller le compte concerné pour repérer toute activité suspecte.
Amazon avait déjà ouvert une adresse équivalente, [email protected], accessible à tous, client ou non.
Consulter le centre de messages de son compte
Un autre excellent réflexe consiste à se connecter directement à son compte en tapant soi-même amazon.fr dans le navigateur, ou en passant par l’application, puis à ouvrir le « Centre de messagerie » depuis la rubrique « Votre compte ».
Tous les mails envoyés par Amazon y sont archivés. Si le message reçu n’y figure pas, il s’agit très probablement d’une arnaque. Pour rappel, Amazon ne demande jamais de payer une commande par virement, par carte cadeau ou en dehors de son site, ni de donner un mot de passe ou un code de vérification par téléphone.
Un ton pressant, qui menace par exemple de bloquer le compte dans l’heure, doit aussi alerter, tout comme une adresse d’expéditeur ou un lien qui ne se termine pas par amazon.fr. Pour voir où mène réellement un lien reçu par mail, il suffit de le survoler avec la souris sur ordinateur, ou de rester appuyé dessus sur mobile.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: Los científicos coinciden: las personas más inteligentes son también las más solitarias por culpa de la evolución
articles.text:
“Tan listo para unas cosas y tan tonto para otras”. Lo que podría ser el tópico espetado a un niño prodigio cuando se le ve fallar en operaciones tan simples como el saber relacionarse con otros niños en el patio de colegio, puede tener en el fondo parte de razón; y lo que es más, raíces biológicas heredadas de siglos y siglos de ancestros. Esto es lo que dice la ciencia sobre los inteligentes tristes y solitarios.
Mejor solo que neciamente acompañado: en 2016 dos investigadores publicaron en el British Journal of Psychology un concienzudo análisis sobre más de 15.000 sujetos y cuyos hallazgos han sido desde entonces muy compartidos: los individuos de alta inteligencia experimentan un nivel de satisfacción personal más bajo cuando socializan con amigos frecuentemente, lo que promueve la reclusión del sujeto.
La teoría de la felicidad de la sabana: los investigadores apoyaban la premisa de que los cerebros de esos sujetos superiores a la media (al menos en lo que se refiere a los campos tradicionalmente asociados con la inteligencia) se habían hecho así por la evolución y la genética. El hombre es un animal social por naturaleza, cuanta más gente tenías a tu alrededor en el pleistoceno mejor debía ser para solucionar conflictos, pero los individuos más listos, alega la psicología evolutiva, se benefician menos de ese contacto social porque son más autónomos.
Esto es hoy más tormentoso que entonces debido a que nuestras sociedades son mucho más grandes y se nos pide que interactuemos con muchas más personas al día que hace miles de años. Si históricamente los humanos nos hemos agrupado en comunidades de entre 150 y 180 individuos, hoy nos movemos rodeados de miles.
Qué pasa cuando eres demasiado listo
Tras la Primera Guerra Mundial el psicólogo Lewis Terman condujo un largo experimento con 1.500 pupilos en California, seleccionados por su elevado cociente intelectual, a los que se acabó apodando Termitas. Pasaron los años y algunos de ellos alcanzaron éxito y fama, sí, pero también muchos de ellos optaron por trabajos normales. La inteligencia y los logros personales no están relacionados, como recordaban las conclusiones del investigador. En este grupo había el mismo porcentaje de divorcios, alcoholismo o suicidio que en el grupo de gente corriente.
Pero lo que sucedió es que al ser preguntados por sus propias vidas, los que tenían un CI más alto se sentían menos realizados con su trayectoria. No habían logrado cumplir sus expectativas vitales, o eran más conscientes de sus propias elecciones desacertadas mirándolas en retrospectiva, algo que se hace doloroso si tenemos en cuenta otro factor: los listos son, de hecho, más incapaces de ver sus flaquezas o aceptar críticas a su conducta en tiempo real.
El velo de la inteligencia les hace ser más ingenuos, o como diríamos de otra forma, se pasan de listillos. Ni que decir tiene que su capacidad de diagnóstico también les hace ver peor el mundo que les rodea. Sus ancestros no sabían que desvinculándose de la tribu acabarían provocando una oleada de ansiedad y depresión.
Con todo, la evidencia más reciente invita a matizar la imagen del genio triste. En 2022, un equipo de la École Normale Supérieure de París comparó a más de 16.000 personas de inteligencia muy alta con otras 236.000 de inteligencia media del UK Biobank y no encontró más trastornos mentales entre los primeros. Al contrario: tenían un 31% menos de probabilidades de sufrir ansiedad generalizada y se sentían menos aislados socialmente.
Y en 2024, un estudio con una muestra representativa de China publicado en el Journal of Happiness Studies concluyó que la relación entre capacidad cognitiva y felicidad es mínima y estadísticamente insignificante: los más inteligentes tienen mejor salud, más ingresos y más estatus, pero tienden a infravalorar su posición y a ver su futuro con menos confianza.
La sabiduría es lo que más se busca: las altas capacidades en determinados ámbitos son lo que llevamos décadas considerando inteligencia, pero cada vez más los expertos apuntan a que deberíamos observar esta cualidad de otra forma, por ejemplo las investigaciones de reclutamiento de Google han descubierto que es más valioso buscar la “humildad intelectual” entre sus candidatos que cualquier otro tipo de distinciones.

articles.title: Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
articles.text:
On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights.
Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
The Steve Jobs of GPUs has been shown the door.
Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now. He has left Nvidia after seemingly enabling two chip smuggling scandals and allegedly having three extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump.
The world is watching to see if this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industry and perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running the first $5 trillion company, he was the visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down.
The 63-year-old once said he preferred to die on the job; he once suggested he’d work until he was 90 or 100, then carry on leading the company as a robot.
It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies. Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO. “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli.
“Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me.
But Nvidia isn’t Jensen anymore. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO.
“He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me.
Elon Musk didn’t exactly found Tesla and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has proven to be neither visionary nor showman so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company dealt with growing employee turmoil, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs.
Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off.
I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a leather jacket; an earlier version was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new.
But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them.
His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processing by firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gun to “paint” the Mona Lisa in one shot.
What I didn’t know back then: Huang was a visionary founder. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets.
In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024.
He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped, The New Yorker wrote in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling a million units in just four months and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and a long-term relationship with chip fabricator TSMC.
Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone. He bet the company’s entire gross profit, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for other kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent.
“Originally there was no market or market demand for it. It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.”
“NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics, with no guarantee of a near-term return,” says HotTech analyst Dave Altavilla.
“Huang saw that a GPU was really a parallel computer that happened to render graphics. CUDA turned that insight into a platform, and it’s why NVIDIA was ready when AI arrived,” Mainelli tells me.
It was a bad time for graphics cards to suddenly cost more. When the Great Recession hit in 2007–2009, and Nvidia laptop graphics chips also started failing due to design defects, the company lost 80 percent of its market value.
But Huang believed in CUDA enough to invest even more. “He literally handed out high-end NVIDIA GPUs to researchers at industry conferences, while the company seeded universities like Stanford with hardware to encourage development on its platform,” says Altavilla. And by 2012, Nvidia’s potential for AI had started to emerge.
That’s when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train a prize-winning image-recognition neural network called AlexNet, which is widely credited for sparking the AI revolution.
Not all of Huang’s visions panned out the way he publicly expected. That AlexNet demo directly led to Huang’s bets on chips for self-driving cars, he said, but he didn’t exactly predict AI — CUDA was instead thought of as better and more affordable supercomputing for researchers and scientists. In 2013, I also wrote about how his grand plan for the future of the company relied heavily on putting Nvidia chips in your phone, which didn’t pan out.
But that bet on ARM-based phone chips did put Nvidia inside every Nintendo Switch and may have helped make future “AI superchips” possible — the latest Nvidia AI server chips have ARM CPU cores. And in 2022, the leaders of the AI revolution launched the most groundbreaking AI tech yet on Nvidia hardware: ChatGPT. Six years earlier, Huang hand-delivered Nvidia’s first purpose-built AI workstation to OpenAI, and by 2022 Microsoft had strung together tens of thousands of Nvidia A100 GPUs to handle the load.
“Every time competitors got close, he moved the fight up a level: the chip, then the server, then networking with the $6.9 billion Mellanox deal, then the full rack, all tied together by CUDA,” says Moorhead. “The speed came from how he ran the company,” he adds. “Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”
“Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”
As Nvidia’s fortunes and profit ballooned — thousands of dollars in pure profit every single second! — and as it became clearer that AI would reshape the world in one way or another, something strange happened. Huang became a celebrity. In summer 2024, The Wall Street Journal and social media chronicled that he received a hero’s welcome in his birthplace of Taiwan. He stopped over and over to sign autographs, including one on a woman’s chest.
In person, at presentations, and in the company’s investor Q&As, I saw the tone shift. People began treating the leather-jacketed man like an actual rockstar instead of a wannabe rockstar, asking for photos and autographs and complimenting him rather than asking tough questions.
It felt like he’d attained Steve Jobs’ infamous “reality distortion field” at last — until he popped that bubble himself with his infidelity.
But one fewer reality distortion field in the world isn’t necessarily a bad thing, and as Apple has shown, a company doesn’t go bust just because its charismatic founder is gone. Tim Cook made Apple the most profitable company in the world. The question now is: who for Nvidia?
“He was the king,” says Peddie. “Make no mistake – it was the Jensen Huang company. He called all the shots, took all the glory, and shouldered all the blame.”
Does Nvidia work without Huang?
Even without a named successor, analysts don’t think Nvidia is in big trouble yet.
“This is a stock shock, not a business shock, for the next year. The roadmap and manufacturing are locked in through 2027,” says Pat Moorhead, Moor Insights & Strategy. “The question is whether Nvidia keeps inventing at Jensen’s pace once those plans run out. The bigger risk than any rival chip is customers hedging during a vacuum. That is why the next CEO needs technical credibility, an operating model that doesn’t depend on one person, and a plan to protect CUDA.”
“Founder visionary, culture setter, leader, AI industry spokesperson etc., is the real loss. We don’t think anything changes strategically,” says Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin.” The product roadmap is set and remains strong, and the next several generations are already in design, in tape-out or on order. NVIDIA is still the company best placed to ship its roadmap at scale, because it has spent years locking up the supply chain behind it, from leading-edge wafers and CoWoS-class packaging to HBM and the rack-level partners. That supply position does not walk out the door with one person.”
“He was the consummate showman, salesman, and visionary for NVIDIA, so he will be hard to replace,” says IDC analyst Tom Mainelli. “But the company’s technology road map is sound, and the team behind him is still there. Choosing the right person to replace him will be key, and there will undoubtedly be bumps along the way. But the company will survive.”
“Jensen built an exceptionally talented organization with a deep engineering bench, a mature, heavily-resourced software ecosystem, and strong customer relationships,” says Dave Altavilla, HotTech Vision and Analysis. “His departure undoubtedly leaves a leadership and strategic vision gap, but the technology, talent, and execution capabilities he helped establish aren’t going away. The real question is whether his successor can sustain that same long-term vision and willingness to invest ahead of the market.”
“No one in the company really wants to step into his shoes, so an outsider is going to have to be found,” says Jon Peddie of Jon Peddie Research. “Whoever that is will not be Jensen, won’t have the same ambitions, the same contacts and relationships, the same vision, or the same courage to make big, long-term bets. We’ve seen this in Apple, AMD, Intel, and other companies. So the stock will probably get battered around a bit until investors see some stability and fewer ‘what if’ questions.”

articles.title: iPad zu Weihnachten: Welches Modell braucht dein Kind wirklich?
articles.text:
iPad-Kaufberatung: Welches Modell sich zu Weihnachten wirklich lohnt
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Bei vielen Schüler:innen hat sich der Wunsch nach einem eigenen Tablet schon erfüllt: Laut Bitkom besaßen 54 Prozent der Sechs- bis 18-Jährigen schon im Jahr 2024 ein eigenes Gerät. In Haushalten, in denen schon ein iPhone oder Macbook vorhanden ist, kann ein iPad besonders praktisch sein, weil es sich nahtlos ins Apple-Ökosystem einfügt. Außerdem bietet es zahlreiche Funktionen, um die Nutzung durch dein Kind im Auge zu behalten. So kannst du unter anderem einen Kinder-Account anlegen, das iPad in die Familienfreigabe aufnehmen, Bildschirmzeiten festlegen und den App- und Webzugriff begrenzen. Wir erklären dir, welches iPad am besten zu deinem Kind passt und mit welchen Kosten du vor Weihnachten rechnen musst.
Unter den Pioneers Picks stellen wir dir regelmäßig weitere praktische Tools und Gadgets vor.
iPad von Apple: Wann das Standardmodell ausreicht
Das Standard-iPad ist ein klassisches Einstiegsmodell und ideal für den Schulalltag. Es verfügt über ein 11 Zoll großes Display. Die Rückkamera mit zwölf Megapixeln filmt in 4K-Qualität. Die Frontkamera bietet ebenfalls zwölf Megapixel. Hinzu kommen Stereo-Lautsprecher und zwei Mikrofone. Die Leistung reicht für Lern-Apps, Notizen und Präsentationen in der Regel aus. Darüber hinaus eignet sich das Apple-Tablet für die meisten Spiele und Entertainment-Apps wie Youtube. Insbesondere für Grundschulkinder und alle, die ihr erstes Tablet bekommen, ist das Standardmodell somit eine gute Wahl.
Das iPad ist mit 128, 256 oder 512 Gigabyte Speicher und einem A16-Chip erhältlich. Laut Hersteller hält der Akku beim Surfen oder Streamen über WLAN bis zu zehn Stunden durch. Es unterstützt den WLAN-Standard 6 und ist optional als SIM-fähige Variante erhältlich. Zubehör wie der Apple Pencil und das Magic Keyboard Folio sind kompatibel. Apple bietet das iPad in Blau, Pink, Gelb und Silber an. Im Apple-Store kostet es Modell 499 Euro in der Basisvariante. Bei Amazon ist das iPad in allen Farben aktuell schon ab 444 Euro erhältlich.
Das zukunftssichere iPad Air für Schule und Studium
Das iPad Air die beste Wahl, wenn du eine leistungsfähige und möglichst langfristige Lösung suchst. Der M4-Chip, der auch in manchen Mac(book)s verbaut ist, bietet mehr Leistung als der A16 im Einstiegsmodell. Das Modell ist mit dieser Ausstattung erst seit März 2026 auf dem Markt und deshalb deutlich zukunftssicherer. Am besten eignet es sich für ältere Kinder in der Mittel- oder Oberstufe. Das iPad Air kann nicht nur bei Hausaufgaben in der Schule unterstützen, sondern dein Kind auch noch beim Start an der Uni begleiten.
Das Tablet ist mit Elf- und 13-Zoll-Display erhältlich. Die Rück- und Frontkamera entsprechen dem Standard-iPad, ebenso die Stereo-Lautsprecher und Mikrofone. Das iPad Air unterstützt allerdings den schnelleren WLAN-Standard 7 und ist als 5G-Mobilfunkversion erhältlich. Zur Auswahl steht es in Dunkelgrau, Türkis, Violett und Gold. Der interne Speicher beträgt maximal ein Terabyte. Laut Hersteller hält der Akku über WLAN bis zu zehn Stunden. Im Apple Store kostet das iPad Air ab 799 Euro. Bei Amazon startet der Preis schon bei 684,81 Euro. Dieser kann je nach Farbe variieren.
iPad kaufen: Was du bei der Auswahl beachten solltest
Apple hat noch weitere Modelle im Portfolio. Das iPad Pro ist auf rechenintensive Workflows wie Video- und Fotobearbeitung oder Grafikdesign zugeschnitten. Für die Schule reicht deshalb meist ein günstigeres Modell aus. Auch das iPad Mini ist für Hausaufgaben und Lernen weniger gut geeignet: Es ist das kompakteste Apple-Tablet und deshalb ideal für unterwegs. Gerade fürs Lesen ist der kleine Bildschirm aber weniger praktisch. Zudem liegt der Preis höher als beim Standardmodell. Als Weihnachtsgeschenk solltest du dich daher zwischen dem „normalen“ iPad und dem iPad Air entscheiden.
Außerdem kann es sich lohnen, mit dem Kauf noch etwas zu warten. Die Angebote von Amazon liegen derzeit zwar deutlich unter der unverbindlichen Preisempfehlung von Apple. Rund um den Black Friday am 27. November sind viele Elektronikartikel aber noch einmal reduziert. Solche Angebote lohnen sich besonders, da Apple aufgrund der anhaltenden Speicherkrise die Preise für einige Produkte deutlich erhöht hat. So kostet das iPad jetzt oft rund 100 Euro mehr als noch vor einigen Monaten. Wer noch mehr sparen möchte, greift zu einem gebrauchten Modell. Auch Kratzer oder Stürze sind hier leichter zu verschmerzen.

articles.title: Is AI Making Us Worse at Cybersecurity?
articles.text:
I was recently asked to speak at an event but was unable to accept due to a prior speaking commitment on the same day. This, in and of itself, is not unusual – it happens fairly often. What happened about a week later, however, gave me some interesting food for thought.
Someone that was available and had agreed to speak at the event in my place approached me to ask for content for the talk. Now, I am always happy to help someone work through what type of content might be interesting and appealing to the audience, as well as to point them in the right direction regarding developing that content. The manner in which this person approached me was not that, unfortunately.
In the moment, I tried to guide the individual in a helpful way. Only later, after analyzing the interaction a bit more, did I realize something. Essentially, the person approached me as people approach AI. How so? Rather than ask for guidance, tips, lessons learned from experience, dos and don’ts, etc., the person basically sent me a prompt. Something that when I thought about it later sounded a lot like “Tell me the most interesting points on topic X and provide me a presentation on that topic.”
This experience got me thinking. Are there ways in which AI could actually be harming us as a security industry? Of course, I know that there are many use cases for which AI helps increase productivity, efficiency, and has other benefits. I am also aware that there are many instances in which attackers are using AI to increase the speed and accuracy with which they attack organizations. What I began asking myself was something fundamentally different – could AI actually be harming the security industry?
The conclusion I came to was yes, it is. While this may sound like a radical stance in 2026, allow me to illustrate through several examples:
- Creativity: While AI can rapidly curate and search through a tremendous amount of data, it is no substitute for human creativity. Most of us recognize the value of creativity in art, music, writing, and other areas. But how many of us appreciate creativity in the security profession? In other words, the creative ways in which security professionals have discovered new things, approached challenges, solved problems, observed irregularities, and noticed oddities? When we use AI for certain security tasks, we lose out on human creativity and all of the benefits that creativity brings, much to our detriment. In my opinion, certain tasks just can’t be taken from a human and given to AI because of this.
- Humor: Humor can be a great way to make a point, diffuse tension, break bad news, and a whole host of other things. Because of this, it is a soft skill that has helped security professionals operate more effectively for decades. When we use AI to create talking points, write for us, create presentations for us, or otherwise, we give up any and all chance for witty humor. I believe this does us a disservice as a profession. Security, like many serious topics, is a medicine best served with a dose of humor to help it go down easier.
- Emotion: AI can mock, mimic, or play to certain human emotions, but it does not feel those emotions. That makes AI feel insincere by nature. Humans are often motivated by sincerity. Many of us are inclined to try harder for people who approach us with genuineness, even if we don’t necessarily want to do or agree with what they are asking of us. The security team that overrotates on AI loses sincerity – arguably one of the most important tools it has.
- Messaging: Recently, while attending a large security conference, I heard quite a few people note that most of the companies on the expo floor were saying all the same things. While this is partly driven by marketing departments looking to use buzzwords that attract attention and drive engagement, there is another aspect here as far as I can tell. It seems that far too many marketing teams are using AI to generate content. Not surprisingly, the messaging that results is unremarkable, non-unique, and woefully unprovoking. We as an industry need messaging that inspires thought, sparks conversation, and remains with people. That means moving away from using AI to help us message.
- Communication: Unfortunately, I’ve noticed a trend towards language becoming less precise and less clear in recent years. There are various forces that I can think of that are contributing to this decline, but AI is definitely one of them. It’s not hard to identify when something has been written by AI, in part or in whole. Security is a profession that is highly dependent on timely and accurate communication. Sadly for us, AI is weakening our communication skills, which is damaging our profession as a whole.
- Critical thinking: In the security field, as in many fields, there are just some situations that no one has encountered before, and for which there is no pre-existing answer. These situations require critical thinking ability. Unfortunately, with so many people in our profession looking to AI to perform analysis for them, offer them suggestions, and organize their thoughts, this important skill is fading. The security profession with an impaired critical thinking capability is not the security profession most of us grew up in.
While the picture may seem grim, all hope is not lost. We can establish firm boundaries for when we will and will not use AI. For example, people who know me know that throughout my career, I have steadfastly refused to use ghostwriters – I write everything that has my name on it. I have continued this principle into the AI era – I won’t use AI to suggest topics, do research for me, organize my thoughts, create an outline, develop any content, or anything else. Perhaps this is old-fashioned, but I believe that it strengthens the quality of the content I put out there, partially due to the reasons shared above. I think that security professionals should resist the temptation that is AI for certain things – we will all benefit from it in the long run.

articles.title: Panne géante : Microsoft balaie la théorie d'un agent IA qui aurait dérapé
articles.text:
On n’a pas encore le fin mot de l’histoire, mais certaines hypothèses sont d’ores et déjà écartées.
Ce vendredi 13 novembre, Microsoft a voulu couper court aux spéculations concernant la panne géante qui a privé des millions d’utilisateurs de Microsoft 365 d’Outlook, de Teams et de plusieurs autres services pendant toute une journée, au point de pousser certaines entreprises à revenir au fax ou à se remettre à passer des coups de fil.
Pas un problème d’IA ou d’agent autonome
Dans un message publié sur son compte X, l’entreprise américaine a écarté la piste d’un raté lié à l’intelligence artificielle (IA). « Il s’agissait d’un problème technique sans rapport avec […] l’IA ou les agents », a écrit le groupe. Les agents IA sont des programmes capables d’enchaîner des tâches de façon autonome, sur la base d’instructions données.
Le géant des logiciels, qui avait déjà écarté la piste d’une cyberattaque, a réaffirmé dans son message qu’aucune attaque informatique n’était liée à cette immense interruption de service. La société se dit « profondément désolée » et promet de « fournir un rapport complet sur cet incident dès que l’examen sera terminé ».
La précision sur les agents se comprend. Microsoft, comme d’autres géants de la tech, pousse les curseurs à fond en faveur de l’intelligence artificielle.
La firme de Redmond met Copilot (l’équivalent de ChatGPT) partout dans ses produits et ses services, elle s’en sert aussi en interne pour améliorer la productivité. En avril 2025, Satya Nadella, le patron du groupe, estimait même que 20 à 30 % du code présent dans les dépôts de Microsoft était écrit par l’IA, une part qui, selon lui, augmentait régulièrement.
De fait, cette tendance à mettre de l’IA partout et à déléguer de plus en plus de travail à l’intelligence artificielle a de quoi alimenter, sur les réseaux sociaux, les théories d’une panne causée par l’automatisation croissante. On y évoquait un bout de code généré par IA, ou une configuration réseau critique qu’aucun humain n’aurait correctement relue.
Une mise à niveau réseau en cause, et peu de détails
Microsoft ferme donc la porte à cette hypothèse, mais le groupe reste encore discret sur les causes profondes de cette perturbation mondiale. À ce stade, d’après l’entreprise, le problème vient d’une « mise à niveau de capacité réseau » faite plus tôt, dont le défaut n’est apparu qu’après « un changement réseau récent ».
Jeudi soir, Microsoft avait déjà décrit le symptôme : sur les serveurs touchés, le processus qui établit les connexions sécurisées était débordé, si bien que les machines ne traitaient plus les demandes. Impossible, par exemple, de se connecter à son compte Outlook, de récupérer les nouveaux mails ou d’en envoyer. Selon les utilisateurs, les services fonctionnaient par intermittence ou pas du tout.
L’entreprise dit avoir corrigé la cause du problème. Elle justifie la lenteur du retour à la normale par un rétablissement progressif, avec un contrôle de stabilité à chaque étape. Pour savoir précisément ce qui a cédé, il faudra attendre le rapport post-incident promis par Microsoft, qui n’a donné aucune date de publication.

articles.title: J’ai remplacé mes enceintes Sonos par le système JBL Cove : pari réussi ou fausse note ?
articles.text:
Quand on s’installe confortablement dans un écosystème audio multiroom, il faut un certain courage (ou en l’occurrence une curiosité journalistique) pour tout balayer d’un revers de main. Propriétaire de longue date d’équipements Sonos, j’ai décidé de franchir le pas en troquant mes fidèles enceintes contre le nouveau système JBL Cove. Un pari orchestré sur une semaine complète de tests intensifs dans toutes les pièces de la maison pour éprouver la solidité de cette nouvelle proposition.
Pour mener à bien cette transition, j’ai redéployé mes pions selon une cartographie précise. Dans le salon, l’imposante JBL Cove X1, vendue à 499 euros, est venue prendre la place de ma Sonos Play:5. Dans la cuisine, c’est la JBL Cove P1, un modèle nomade affiché à 449 euros, qui a détrôné ma Sonos Move. Enfin, dans la salle de bain, la compacte JBL Cove M1, facturée 229 euros, a remplacé ma vénérable Sonos One.
Cette configuration éclectique m’a permis de couvrir l’ensemble des cas de figure du quotidien : écoute intimiste dans une seule pièce, diffusion simultanée dans toute la maison, lancement de flux depuis un smartphone ou encore requêtes vocales via Alexa. Mais avant de juger sur pièces, penchons-nous sur ce que nous promet le constructeur américain.
Une gamme triplement armée : décorticage technique
Annoncée le 1er septembre 2026, la gamme JBL Cove ambitionne de redéfinir les standards de l’audio domestique en mariant la signature sonore de la marque à une flexibilité moderne. Au cœur de cette proposition, trois références bien distinctes qui affichent des ambitions techniques musclées.
En haut de la pyramide, la JBL Cove X1 (499 euros) s’impose comme le modèle emblématique. Avec ses dimensions de 26 x 17,8 x 17,2 cm pour un poids net de 4,88 kg, cette enceinte domestique Wi-Fi diffuse un son 3D immersif compatible Dolby Atmos. Sous son capot, elle intègre un arsenal acoustique impressionnant : deux woofers de 3,5 x 4,7 pouces (90 x 120 mm) et quatre tweeters de 1,25 pouce (30 mm), dont certains orientés vers le haut pour propager les effets verticaux.
Juste en dessous, la JBL Cove P1 (449 euros) se distingue par sa portabilité. Pesant 3,26 kg pour des mensurations de 14,6 x 23,3 x 14,7 cm, elle intègre une architecture audio 3.0.1 délivrant 120 W de puissance totale RMS. Elle embarque un woofer de 105 mm, un haut-parleur haute fréquence de 20 mm et trois haut-parleurs haute fréquence de 30 mm. Sa botte secrète ? Une batterie lithium de 4 800 mAh offrant jusqu’à 14 heures d’autonomie, un indice de protection IP56 garantissant une résistance à l’eau et à la poussière, ainsi qu’une station de charge dédiée.
Enfin, la JBL Cove M1 (229 euros) joue la carte de la compacité avec ses 12,5 x 18,4 x 12,5 cm et ses 1,65 kg. Malgré son format réduit, elle intègre un woofer de 105 mm et trois tweeters de 20 mm, assurant une écoute quotidienne fluide et détaillée.
Toutes trois bénéficient des technologies propriétaires de la marque : le Constant Sound Field pour un équilibre sonore homogène dans toute la pièce, l’AI Sound Boost pour minimiser la distorsion à volume élevé, ainsi qu’un calibrage automatique s’adaptant à l’acoustique de l’environnement. Côté connectivité, la prise en charge est totale : Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3 compatible Auracast, AirPlay, Google Cast, Roon Ready, Spotify Connect, Tidal Connect et Qobuz Connect.
Installation et configuration : l’écosystème JBL One en chef d’orchestre
L’installation d’un système multiroom se doit d’être une formalité, sous peine de rebuter l’utilisateur dès les premières minutes. Sur ce point, JBL remplit son contrat. La configuration initiale des trois enceintes s’est révélée d’une grande simplicité grâce à l’application JBL One.
Cette application, conçue pour devenir la plaque tournante de tous les appareils de la marque (qu’il s’agisse de casques, d’enceintes nomades ou de barres de son), guide l’utilisateur pas à pas. En quelques minutes, les enceintes ont rejoint sans encombre le réseau Wi-Fi domestique. L’interface de l’application s’avère claire, permettant d’accéder rapidement aux réglages d’égalisation, à la mise en page des groupes d’écoute et aux services de streaming.
Un point particulièrement intéressant pour les possesseurs d’équipements home-cinéma de la marque : les enceintes JBL Cove peuvent s’associer sans fil aux barres de son JBL Bar Series MK2 pour officier en tant que canaux arrière surround, garantissant une configuration Dolby Atmos unifiée au sein du salon.
L’ergonomie générale du système se veut fluide. Pour diffuser de la musique dans toute la maison, il suffit de regrouper les enceintes depuis l’application JBL One. À l’inverse, pour une écoute cloisonnée, chaque enceinte fonctionne de manière autonome dans son espace dédié.
Fonctionnalités et ergonomie : « Master and Servant »
Au quotidien, l’utilisation des JBL Cove révèle un mélange de fulgurances ergonomiques et de choix de conception déroutants, notamment pour un utilisateur aguerri aux habitudes de la concurrence.
Parmi les fonctionnalités phares, la technologie Music Follows Me tire parti du bouton « Moment » présent sur le dessus des enceintes. Une pression longue sur ce bouton permet à la musique de suivre l’utilisateur d’une pièce à l’autre, se connectant à la volée à la diffusion en cours sans avoir à ressortir son smartphone de sa poche. De même, la prise en charge de Spotify Tap via ce même bouton facilite l’accès direct à ses playlists.
Cependant, le comportement en mode multiroom réserve quelques surprises. Le fonctionnement de type « maître-esclave » adopté par JBL s’avère pour le moins déroutant. Lorsque l’on presse le bouton pause sur une enceinte secondaire (esclave), la lecture s’interrompt uniquement sur cette dernière, et non sur l’ensemble du groupe, contrairement à ce que propose Sonos. Plus curieux encore : si l’on relance la lecture sur cette même enceinte esclave après l’avoir mise en pause, c’est le contenu qu’elle lisait précédemment qui se relance, et non le flux synchrone de l’enceinte maîtresse.
Du côté des services de streaming intégrés nativement dans l’application, l’offre se montre encore un peu chiche avec seulement six services pris en charge (notamment Amazon Music, Qobuz et Tidal), omettant des géants comme Spotify ou Apple Music dans l’interface directe, obligeant à passer par AirPlay ou Cast.
Durant ma semaine de test, j’ai également constaté quelques micro-coupures occasionnelles ainsi que de légers décalages de synchronisation entre les enceintes, générant un effet d’écho passager. Des soucis vraisemblablement d’ordre logiciel, qui, espérons-le, seront corrigés par de futures mises à jour de firmware. Enfin, l’assistant vocal Alexa intégré montre des limites agaçantes : il est impossible de lui ordonner de diffuser de la musique sur une enceinte spécifique ou sur l’ensemble du parc à la voix.
Qualité audio : la signature JBL face à la neutralité Sonos
Abordons le nerf de la guerre : que vaut réellement ce système sur le plan acoustique ? La réponse dépend étroitement de vos goûts musicaux et de votre sensibilité auditive.
Fidèle à sa réputation, JBL nous livre ici une signature sonore typique en « V », très démonstrative et résolument vivante. La JBL Cove X1 dans le salon impressionne par sa capacité à remplir l’espace. Les basses sont profondes, percutantes, et l’apport du Dolby Atmos procure une sensation d’enveloppement sur les pistes compatibles qui dépasse largement les limites physique de l’appareil. La JBL Cove P1 dans la cuisine fait des merveilles avec une puissance surprenante pour sa taille, tandis que la petite M1 assure dans la salle de bain une clarté vocale irréprochable, parfaite pour écouter la radio sous la douche le matin. Le calibrage automatique remplit par ailleurs très bien son office pour dompter les réverbérations des pièces exiguës.
Pourtant, comparé à la rigueur et à la douceur plus neutre d’un système Sonos, le rendu des JBL peut parfois sembler un brin artificiel ou exubérant. Là où Sonos mise sur un équilibre feutré qui ne fatigue jamais l’oreille sur la durée, JBL privilégie l’impact immédiat et l’énergie brute qui peut être fatigante pour les oreilles à la longue. Les amateurs de sensations fortes et de pop, de rock ou d’electro aux basses généreuses y trouveront leur compte ; les puristes de la hi-fi acoustique la plus rigoureuse regretteront un léger manque de subtilité dans les registres médiums.
Verdict : faut-il lâcher Sonos pour JBL Cove ?
Au terme de cette semaine d’immersion, l’heure du bilan a sonné. Le système JBL Cove constitue une alternative crédible et solidement construite sur le marché encombré du multiroom.
Côté tarifaire, JBL se positionne de manière agressive : la M1 est proposée au même tarif que la Sonos Era 100 (229 euros), tandis que la P1 (449 euros) et la X1 (499 euros) s’affichent toutes deux 50 euros moins cher que leurs équivalentes directes chez Sonos (la Move 2 à 499 euros et l’Era 300 à 549 euros).
Le système JBL Cove séduit par sa simplicité d’installation, la polyvalence de ses modèles (notamment la portabilité de la P1) et la générosité de sa restitution sonore. Toutefois, l’ergonomie logicielle de son mode multiroom maître-esclave et ses quelques aspérités de synchronisation demandent un temps d’adaptation pour qui est habitué à la fluidité plus transparente de l’écosystème Sonos.
Si vous cherchez un son démonstratif, des fonctionnalités nomades bien pensées et un rapport qualité-prix légèrement plus avantageux, le pari est gagné. Si vous ne jurez que par la logique implacable du multiroom historique et une signature sonore plus douce, la transition méritera mûre réflexion.

articles.title: US disrupts North Korean campaign behind $400 million crypto theft
articles.text:
The U.S. government has disrupted a North Korean social engineering campaign called ‘FaceStealer’, responsible for stealing more than $400 million in cryptocurrency.
The attacks used multiple social engineering techniques, including deepfakes and ClickFix, to target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors, as well as open-source developers.
The FaceStealer campaign ran for 18 months before the U.S. seized the underlying cloud-based infrastructure.
U.S. authorities identified more than 900 webcam videos that hackers secretly recorded of tech workers, who were deceived in the massive North Korean operation.
An FBI alert earlier this week notes that the North Korean threat actor hijacked accounts on Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord, and used them to invite victims to video meetings under various pretenses.
During the video calls, the attacker showed recorded footage of people the targets knew and who had previously fallen victim, too.
The FBI explains that while the target waited for the meeting to start, the hacker secretly recorded a video, which was later used with other targets. The meeting sometimes featured recordings of multiple familiar individuals to add pressure on the current victim in the next stage.
Shortly after, the hacker claimed a technical issue and displayed a fake error message to justify delivering a malicious “fix.”
The target was then prompted to follow a link that purported to offer a fix, such as an update or installer, which infected their computer with malware that steals crypto data and account credentials for video meeting platforms such as Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams.
The malware also provides access to the victims' contact lists, social media, communication apps, and webcam videos.
According to the FBI, attackers sometimes delayed targeting individuals for months or even more than a year after the initial compromise, likely waiting for their cryptocurrency holdings to grow.
ArticWolf researchers attributed the FaceStealer campaign to the BlueNoroff hacker group and listed additional lures, including financial documents, fake PDF viewer updates, identity verification prompts, and security audits, all designed to persuade the target to run a “fix.”
The researchers identified 677 targets across 58 countries, with a heavy focus on company founders and senior executives.
Huntress cybersecurity company attributed a similar campaign to BlueNoroff in 2025, where the attackers used Zoom calls to infect company executives with custom macOS malware.
The FBI bulletin highlighted an incident in which the hackers compromised the maintainer of a popular open-source JavaScript library with tens of millions of weekly downloads, after luring them into a fake Teams meeting with multiple participants, including one familiar to the developer.
The attack was thwarted thanks to quick detection, but the FBI says it confirmed multiple other attempts against developers in the npm and Rust crate ecosystems.
Amazon threat analysts also attributed several open-source software supply chain attacks to BlueNoroff in a July 2026 report.
To defend against these attacks, users are recommended to join meetings only through official apps using an invite code, verify unexpected invitations independently, and keep the webcam off unless explicitly needed. Finally, avoid running scripts offered as fixes to technical problems.
As a separate announcement, the U.S. Justice Department said that together with private sector companies, the U.S. government froze more than $2.7 billion from the 6.4 billion Binance crypto heist.
The DoJ has already "obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount."
