articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

articles.title: Apple Reveals How Secure Exclaves Shield Camera and Microphone Data
articles.text:
Apple has published a detailed description of Secure Exclaves, a security architecture in its silicon designed to keep camera and microphone data used for ambient sensing isolated from the main operating system.
Ambient sensing lets a device listen for “Hey Siri”. On the recently introduced HomeView smart display, it enables the recognition of user faces and voices.
Secure Exclaves are isolated runtimes that handle camera and microphone data apart from the rest of the device.
“Isolation features added across many core components of the silicon work in tandem to protect Secure Exclaves and keep them segregated from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in a Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple,” the company said.
The design is built around three requirements. The main OS must not be able to pull out or alter data handled in an exclave, and only a narrowly defined set of information may cross over to it. Users must also be able to tell when a sensor session is active, without the main OS interfering.
According to Apple, in background sensing only specific metadata reaches the rest of the system. On HomeView, the recognition result sent to the main OS is a person identifier, position and confidence level, without audio or video data being shared.
When an app requests full sensor access, a dedicated exclave acts as gatekeeper. Sensor data is released only once it has confirmed the indicator is on and has been showing for a sufficient period.
On devices such as the iPhone, where the indicator is an on-screen dot, another exclave checks which pixels were actually drawn to the display.
Apple said Secure Exclaves protect person recognition on HomeView, along with Siri Recap and Live Rewind. They also protect the on-screen camera and microphone indicators in iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo, and the camera indicators in MacBook Neo and HomeView.
The exclaves run on a minimal, capability-based microkernel, to which Apple has been applying formal verification. Apple said this turned up hard-to-spot but critical flaws in many kernel subsystems that could have led to full kernel compromise. Many of these issues were caught early in development.
The microkernel is still under active development and changes often, Apple noted. “Because of these constant changes, we do not claim complete coverage of all aspects of the kernel; instead, formal verification is applied gradually and incrementally to different parts,” it said.

articles.title: Ticket zum Saturn: Schicke deinen Namen mit der NASA zum Titan
articles.text:
Dein Name auf dem Saturnmond: So schickst du ihn mit der NASA zum Titan
2028 soll die Helikopterdrohne Dragonfly auf ihre Reise in Richtung Titan starten. Ab 2034 soll sie dann den größten Mond des Saturn erforschen.
Virtuelle Bordkarte und dein Name auf deinem Chip
Du kannst bei der Mission dabei sein – zumindest virtuell. Die Nasa hat eine Homepage aktiviert, auf der du deinen Namen hinterlassen kannst. Der wird dann auf einen Chip an Bord der Dragonfly eingraviert.
Wenn du auf der Seite Vor-, Nachname und deine E‑Mail-Adresse eingibst, erhältst du außerdem eine personalisierte Bordkarte für den Trip. Du bekommst dann laut Nasa Updates zu der Mission geschickt und nimmst teil an einem virtuellen Gastprogramm.
Name bis Mitte Januar 2027 hinterlassen
Wer dabei sein will, hat noch gut zwei Monate Zeit, um seinen Namen verewigen zu lassen. Die Frist endet am 15. Januar 2027.
Die Publicity-Aktion ist Ende Oktober dieses Jahres gestartet. Bis jetzt haben sich schon über 350 000 Menschen registriert (Stand: 9. November 2026).
Standortwechsel alle ein-zwei Titan-Tage
Die Nasa hat die Mission von Dragonfly im Sommer 2019 angekündigt. Damals war von einem Launch im Jahr 2026 die Rede, später verschob die US-Raumfahrtbehörde den Start um zwei Jahre.
Der Helikopter soll an Bord einer Falcon Heavy von SpaceX zum Titan fliegen. Auf dem zweitgrößten Mond des Sonnensystems soll er innerhalb von drei Jahren an mehreren Orten landen und Bodenproben sammeln.
Geplant sind Standortwechsel alle ein bis zwei Titan-Tage. Ein Tag auf dem Saturnmond entspricht 16 Tagen auf der Erde. In der Zeit dazwischen muss die Drohne ihre Batterien aufladen.
Dragonfly: 450 Kilo in 4000 Metern Höhe
Dragonfly ist etwa so groß wie ein SUV. Er besitzt acht Rotoren, die das fast 450 Kilogramm schwere Gefährt auf eine Flughöhe von bis zu 4000 Metern bringen können.
Die Kameras der Drohne wurden bereits auf dem Mars getestet. Betrieben wird Dragonfly nuklear und verwendet dabei ein System, das dem der Marsrover sehr ähnlich ist: den Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator.
Das verspricht sich die Nasa von der Titan-Mission
Warum ausgerechnet Titan? Der Mond verfügt über eine Atmosphäre, Flüsse und Seen, Jahreszeiten und eine Landschaft, die reich an organischem Material ist.
Titan ähnelt laut dem Stand der Forschung der ursprünglichen, methanreichen Erde. Seine Erforschung könnte also Aufschlüsse dafür liefern, wie auf unserem Planeten Leben entstanden ist.

articles.title: Aucune sonde n'a jamais été aussi loin dans le cosmos : Voyager 1 arrive à un jour lumière de la Terre, et la NASA lance un jeu
articles.text:
C’est désormais imminent. Le mercredi 18 novembre, à 11h16 (heure de Paris), Voyager 1 sera à une distance d’un jour lumière de la Terre. Ce jalon, que l’on surveille depuis maintenant un an, sera symbolique. D’abord parce que l’on peut désormais changer d’échelle d’unité. Ensuite, parce qu’aucun objet fabriqué par l’humanité n’est allé aussi loin.
Il faut saisir ce que cela veut dire : à un jour lumière de la Terre, cela signifie que la lumière partie de la planète bleue met 24 heures pour rejoindre la sonde. Une journée entière. Et il faut une autre journée pour faire le chemin en sens inverse. Pour les échanges radio, qui filent à la vitesse de la lumière, un échange prend donc deux jours.
En comparaison, la lumière du Soleil met environ huit minutes à atteindre la Terre. Pluton, c’est cinq heures et demie. Cela donne une bonne idée du trajet effectué par la sonde : presque 26 milliards de kilomètres, en filant à 61 155 km/h. C’est tout à fait vertigineux, mais ce n’est pas demain la veille que Voyager 1 atteindra un autre système solaire.
Il a fallu du temps pour atteindre ce cap. Voyager 1 a été lancée en 1977 et traverse le cosmos depuis bientôt cinquante ans. En 2012, elle est sortie de l’héliosphère, la bulle de particules que le Soleil gonfle autour de lui, et elle est entrée dans l’espace interstellaire. Il s’agit d’une zone qui n’est plus sous l’influence directe de notre étoile.
Pour marquer le coup, l’agence spatiale a annoncé un petit jeu : saluer la sonde avec une lampe torche ou avec son smartphone.
Comment faire signe à Voyager 1 mardi soir
Le mardi 17 novembre, une fois le soleil couché, ouvrez l’application dédiée de la NASA (un site clignotant, qu’on trouve aussi sur la page « Shine Bright » de la NASA) dans le navigateur d’un smartphone ou d’une tablette, puis pointez l’appareil vers le ciel. La page fera clignoter en morse les lettres « VGR », l’indicatif de la mission.
Si vous préférez le faire à la main avec une lampe, alternez des éclats brefs (les points) et des éclats d’environ une seconde (les traits), avec une courte pause entre deux éclats et au moins une seconde entre deux lettres. Le V s’écrit trois brefs et un long, le G deux longs et un bref, le R un bref, un long et un bref.
Pour celles et ceux qui le désirent, la NASA propose de photographier ou filmer le signal et à le publier sur les réseaux sociaux en citant la @NASA. Attention, c’est surtout une vague de lumière poétique et symbolique : l’agence prévient qu’aucune lampe de poche ne sera captée par Voyager 1 à près de 26 milliards de kilomètres.
Le 19 novembre à 18 heures (heure de Paris), le Jet Propulsion Laboratory, le centre de la NASA qui pilote les deux sondes Voyager, diffusera sur nasa.gov/live une table ronde avec l’équipe de la mission. On y verra aussi un premier extrait du documentaire que la NASA prépare pour NASA+, sa plateforme vidéo, attendu en 2027 pour les 50 ans de la mission.

articles.title: No Signs of Hacking in FAA Ground Stop as FBI Reportedly Probes Software Update
articles.text:
US officials have found no evidence that hackers caused the outage that led the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to halt flight departures nationwide on Friday, and the FBI is reportedly examining whether a software update was responsible.
The FAA issued the ground stop on November 13 after a communications problem hit its air route traffic control centers. The order was lifted at 8:15 pm ET, more than four hours later, after disrupting thousands of flights. Departures have since resumed, though officials expect delays to continue for several days.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that the incident did not appear to be the result of a cyberattack, and that the failure appeared to be mechanical.
On the absence of attack indicators, Mullin said “there’s no chatter, we haven’t seen any footprints.”
He stopped short of dismissing the possibility entirely. “However, we’re still looking, so we’re not going to rule that out,” Mullin said.
The NSA, the Department of Defense, CISA and other agencies have been involved in the investigation, according to Mullin.
The FBI does not think a cyberattack or criminal activity was behind the outage, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. Investigators are looking at a software update as a potential cause, the source said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed legacy equipment. He said switches and routers in the FAA’s network were flooded with data and began producing inconsistent information, at which point the agency shut the system down.
Officials described the ground stop as a precaution.
Mullin offered a possible trigger. He said it appeared the FAA had been applying patches and installing new equipment and technology, which “was overwhelming the older system.”
CBS News, citing multiple sources, reported that the outage followed an update to the private communications network that links the air traffic control system. The network rebooted and then crashed, and it is operated by L3Harris, according to the report.
Officials said the incident had nothing to do with the Microsoft outage earlier in the week. They also said the FAA’s recently deployed AI systems played no role.
No official root cause has been announced.
The previous nationwide ground stop came in January 2023, after a contractor unintentionally deleted files while working on the system that delivers safety notices to pilots. No evidence of a cyberattack was found in that case either.

articles.title: AMD Launches EPYC Embedded 9006: Venice Gets an Early Start in Embedded
articles.text:
Last week we witnessed the launch of AMD’s EPYC 9006 “Venice” series of server CPUs. AMD’s latest generation of server chips, the Venice launch marked an important inflection point on AMD’s server CPU business for a few different reasons. Not only was it the company’s first Zen 6 architecture chip family with all of the performance and feature benefits that entails, but it also marked a larger shift in AMD’s business. For the Zen 6 generation, at least, servers are now coming first for the company – and what was once one of the last products to launch with a new architecture is now the first.
That shift towards prioritizing servers was not just for AMD’s commercial operations, either. Alongside the company’s standard EPYC 9006, AMD went one step further and launched their EPYC Embedded 9006 chip family as well. The highly validated variant of AMD’s server chips that is meant for more foundational roles has never before launched at the same time as the traditional commercial chips, underscoring just how much things have changed for AMD in the past couple of years.
It also means that we have a whole other EPYC product stack to talk about, and one that is aimed at a somewhat different market segment to boot.
Though whether it is commercial EPYC or EPYC embedded, AMD’s technical strengths remain the same. The Venice SP7 platform brings with it significant increases in core counts, energy efficiency, I/O bandwidth, memory bandwidth, and more. And AMD expects that its embedded customers are just as much in need of the extra performance as the rank and file (and AI) customers who have been scooping up standard EPYC chips.
AMD EPYC Embedded 9006 Overview
These days, AMD’s complete EPYC embedded portfolio stretches from chips with a handful of cores all the way up to 256 cores, reaching parity with AMD’s best server chips. The higher-end chips have always been derived from AMD’s server and desktop platforms, and that has not changed for the EPYC Embedded 9006 series.
In this case, the embedded version of the 9006 Venice family is adopting the SP7 platform wholesale. Which means it gets access to features such as 16 channel DDR5-8000/MRDRIMM-12800 support, 96 lanes of PCIe Gen6/CXL 3.1, the Zen 6/Zen 6c architectures, and AMD’s suite of security features for enterprise computing.
| AMD EPYC Embedded: Generation on Generation |  |  |  | 
|  | Embedded 9004 | Embedded 9005 | Embedded 9006 | 
| Codename | Genoa | Turin | Venice | 
| Microarchitecture | Zen 4 | Zen 5c | Zen 6c | 
| Core Manufacturing | 5nm | 3nm | 2nm | 
| Max Cores/Threads | 128/256 | 192/384 | 256/512 | 
| Core Complex | 16 + 32MB | 16 + 32MB | 32 + 128MB | 
| Memory Support | 12x DDR5-4800 | 12x DDR5-6400 | 16x DDR5-8000 / MRDIMM-12800 | 
| Memory Capacity | 6TB | 6TB | 8TB | 
| PCIe (1P) | 5.0 x128 | 5.0 x128 | 6.0 x96 | 
| Socket | SP5 | SP5 | SP7 | 
| Peak Power | 400W | 500W | 600W | 
Where the EPYC Embedded 9006 lineup will chiefly differ from AMD’s commercial server operations is in regard to the chip availability and product support lifecycles. AMD will offer the 9006 embedded chips for at least 7 years, and they will be supporting the chips for longer.
As well, the upgrade to the SP7 platform means that AMD’s embedded customers now get to reset the clock in terms of upgradability as compared to the SP5 platform. AMD will be reusing the SP7 platform for the next generation of chips (codenamed Florence), which means that designs being created today can be reused/upgraded in the future to use the newer chips without having to redesign or revalidate the entire platform.
All of which are important features for AMD’s target market of embedded users, who, even more than commercial server customers, move at a slower, more deliberate and conservative pace with their hardware designs and release cadences. The typical goal being to release a design for years, and support it for even longer.
Target Markets: ATE, Firewalls, and Enterprise Storage
Though the EPYC Embedded 9006 processors are being made available to AMD’s entire embedded customer base, the company has a few specific ideas in mind for what the best classes of products are for the new EPYC chips. Especially with the top-end of the new 9006 stack pushing total compute throughput harder than ever, these are the workloads that AMD (and its marketing arm) have been looking at.
Broadly speaking, AMD is chasing three particular markets with EPYC Embedded 9006: automatic test equipment (ATE) for semiconductor development, high-end firewalls, and enterprise storage controllers. All of which fall under the umbrella of long-lived infrastructure, and all of which are also tangential to the AI market in some form or another.
Firewalls are the most straightforward. With agentic AI systems pushing around more data than ever, faster firewalls are needed to keep up, be it by processing more data or being able to handle more complex (and thus CPU-intensive) policies. Even with the significant amount of offload acceleration in firewall appliances, they can still be quite CPU-intensive.
Similarly, AI computing demand is driving up storage demand as well. With rackscale systems making heavy use of dedicated storage boxes, a fast CPU is needed to operate those storage systems – and AMD would like it to be theirs. Coupled with that, the 9006 family marks the introduction of PCIe Gen6 support on AMD’s EPYC Embedded platform, so for storage systems that are not using a PCIe switch of some kind, native PCIe Gen6 support is the key to getting the most out of the first generation of PCIe Gen6 SSDs.
Finally, in a less conventional role, AMD is targeting the ATE market in this generation of EPYC Embedded. Automatic test equipment is not normally a very visible market, as the need for equipment is clustered around engineering firms rather than the hyperscalers, neoclouds, and other data centers that are deploying hardware in large volumes. But according to AMD, they are expecting a fresh jump in demand here due to all of the new technologies in play with this generation of hardware. Faster DDR5 RDIMMs, MRDIMMs, PCIe Gen6/CXL 3.1, and more. All of which will require new component designs and then significant validation of those designs.
More than anything else, this one seems to be AMD flexing at being among the first vendors to make a server processor with all of these features widely available. Intel is months away, and the various Arm-based operations are still ramping up their own hardware.
Though for AMD Embedded customers who are making heavy use of PCIe connectivity, they will have to contend with a bit less of it overall. While the SP5 platform supported 128 lanes of PCIe Gen5, the SP7 platform only supports 96 lanes of PCIe Gen6 – so while the lanes are faster, there are fewer of them overall.
Final Words
Wrapping things up, with this month’s launch of their Venice server chips and their related EPYC product lines, we are seeing first-hand how AMD’s processor releases cadences have shifted significantly. With an emphasis on getting server processors out the door first, the lead products for a new CPU microarchitecture have become the EPYC family. And not just AMD’s standard commercial chips, but their EPYC Embedded chips as well, bringing the latter line from one of the last to launch to one of the first. It is a major change that goes to show just how important the EPYC Embedded lineup has become to AMD’s overall plans.
As for how AMD’s embedded customers will put the new chips and all of their new features to good use, the wait should not be very long, either. AMD is already making the 128 core EPYC Embedded 9756 available this month. The other 5 chips will quickly follow in late December.

articles.title: Xiaomi Electric Scooter 4 Ultra : la trottinette aux 70 km d'autonomie perd un tiers de son prix
articles.text:
Présentée au MWC de Barcelone en 2023, la Xiaomi Electric Scooter 4 Ultra n’est certes plus le modèle le plus récent de la marque chinoise, mais elle reste une très bonne trottinette électrique. Malgré l’arrivée de la nouvelle génération, avec notamment la Xiaomi Electric Scooter 5 Pro, elle conserve de solides arguments, en particulier pour les trajets longs grâce à sa conception robuste et à son autonomie généreuse. À l’occasion du pré-Black Friday, son prix baisse : une bonne occasion de s’offrir un modèle encore très convaincant sans forcément investir dans la dernière génération.
Sur sa boutique officielle du fabricant, l’Electric Scooter 4 Ultra s’affiche à 399,99 € au lieu de 599,99 €. Ça fait 200 € de moins, soit un tiers du prix de référence, et 600 € de moins que son prix de 999,99 € à sa sortie en 2023.
C’est quoi, la Xiaomi Electric Scooter 4 Ultra ?
Ce modèle embarque un moteur de 500 W en puissance nominale, et peut monter jusqu’à 940 W en pointe, sur de courts instants, pour une accélération ou une côte jusqu’à 25 %. La vitesse reste bridée à 25 km/h, la limite légale pour une trottinette électrique en France. Quatre modes sont disponibles, du mode piéton à 6 km/h jusqu’au mode S+, qui libère toute la puissance pour atteindre plus vite les 25 km/h.
Niveau confort, la trottinette a une double suspension, à l’avant et à l’arrière, et des pneus tubeless de 10 pouces. Le guidon est plus large et plus haut que sur les modèles plus simples de la marque, et le plateau plus grand. Elle supporte jusqu’à 120 kg et elle est certifiée IPX5, donc elle résiste aux projections d’eau d’une averse. Un confort qui a un coût : la trottinette pèse environ 24,5 kg.
La batterie de 561,5 Wh permet 70 km d’autonomie environ, selon la taille et le poids de l’usager, le relief et la vitesse. Il faut s’attendre à moins au quotidien, surtout par temps froid.
À ce prix, la Xiaomi Electric Scooter 4 Ultra est-elle une bonne affaire ?
À 399,99 €, la Xiaomi Electric Scooter 4 Ultra est une excellente affaire, surtout si vos trajets sont assez longs ou vous font passer par des pavés et des chaussées abîmées. Elle offre même quelques arguments face à la plus récente Xiaomi Electric Scooter 5 Pro : une batterie plus généreuse (561,5 Wh contre 477 Wh) et une autonomie annoncée supérieure (70 km contre 60 km). Les deux modèles proposent une double suspension et une vitesse maximale de 25 km/h. Autrement dit, pour des prestations assez proches, payer seulement 399,99 € pour la 4 Ultra est particulièrement intéressant.
Au final, vous économisez 200 € par rapport à son prix habituel de 599,99 €. De quoi garder un peu de budget pour acheter un bon casque ou un antivol sérieux.
Black Friday 2026 : tout ce qu’il faut savoir
Depuis une dizaine d’années, le Black Friday s’est infiltré dans le calendrier commercial des grandes marques et enseignes françaises. Avec l’expérience, on peut vous dire que cet événement fait partie des meilleurs moments pour faire de bonnes affaires.
Les dates du Black Friday
Bien qu’il porte encore le nom du vendredi noir, le Black Friday s’étend désormais sur un mois chez de nombreux revendeurs. Un format moins typique qui lui retire un peu son petit côté FOMO. On dirait presque les soldes, finalement. Mais c’est aussi moins le rush, ce qui est une bonne chose pour ceux qui veulent faire des achats plus raisonnés. Globalement, on peut résumer ce Black Friday en quatre temps forts :
- Début novembre : les avant-premières Black Friday.
- Autour du 20 novembre, selon les enseignes : la Black Week commence généralement plusieurs jours avant le jour J.
- 27 novembre : la date du Black Friday, même si les offres commencent généralement avant et se prolongent le week-end des 28 et 29 novembre.
- 30 novembre : le Cyber Monday.
